Let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(j\ge1\), fix a nonzero element \(\xi\in\mathbb Q_\ell(j)\), and let \(m'\ge m\) be divisible by \(m\). Let \(Z_1,\dots,Z_s\) be closed integral subschemes of \(X_{\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}}\) of pure codimension \(j\), and for each \(i\) let \(\mathrm{cl}(Z_i)\in H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the unique vector whose tensor with \(\xi\) is the \(\ell\)-adic cycle class of the base change of \(Z_i\) to \(k\) in \(H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j))\). Let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}\), and let \(W\subseteq H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-span of the classes \(F^t(\mathrm{cl}(Z_i))\) for \(1\le i\le s\) and all \(t\ge0\). Then \(W\) is \(F\)-stable and, for every embedding \(\iota:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\) and every eigenvalue \(\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) of \(F|_W\), one has \(\iota(\alpha)\overline{\iota(\alpha)}=q^{2mj}\).
proof:
Write Q := q^m = p^{am}, which is again a prime power, and r := m'/m, which is an integer ≥1 because m' ≥ m and m \mid m'. Then ℙ_{q^{m'}} = ℙ_{Q^r}, and k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q is simultaneously an algebraic closure of \mathbb F_q and of \mathbb F_{q^m} = \mathbb F_Q. The operator F in the statement is F = (\mathrm{id}_{X_k} \times \operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^* with \sigma(c) = c^{q^m} = c^{Q}, i.e. it is the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius for the \mathbb F_Q-structure on X.

**Step 0 (F is a well-defined \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphism of H^{2j}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)).** Since every element of \mathbb F_Q = \mathbb F_{q^m} satisfies c^{q^m} = c, the automorphism \sigma:k\to k restricts to the identity on the field of definition \mathbb F_Q of X; hence the square
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
X_k & \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma\ } & X_k\\
\downarrow & & \downarrow\\
\operatorname{Spec}k & \xrightarrow{\ \operatorname{Spec}\sigma\ } & \operatorname{Spec}k
\end{array}
\]
commutes over \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_Q, so \mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma is a well-defined \sigma-semilinear automorphism of the k-scheme X_k, and its pullback on \acute etale cohomology is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear operator. Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a with the ground field \mathbb F_Q in place of \mathbb F_q (so that its "q-power field automorphism" is exactly our \sigma, since \sigma(a)=a^Q=a^{q^m}), we obtain that F = F_{ar} is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphism of H^{2j}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob likewise with \mathbb F_Q in place of \mathbb F_q (X is proper over \mathbb F_Q, and Q_\ell is equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism) gives that V := H^{2j}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell.

**Step 1 (the classes cl(Z_i) are exactly those of Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_314).** In Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_314, with the base prime power q replaced by Q, with X (smooth projective over \mathbb F_Q), with the same integer j \ge 1 (the lemma allows j \ge 0), with the same fixed nonzero \xi \in \mathbb Q_\ell(j), with the extension degree m of that lemma replaced by our r \ge 1, and with Z_0 = Z_i \subseteq X_{\mathbb F_{Q^r}} = X_{\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}}, the class produced by that lemma is "the unique vector whose tensor with \xi is the \ell-adic cycle class of the base change of Z_i to k in H^{2j}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j))". This is verbatim the definition of \mathrm{cl}(Z_i) in the present statement. Thus the hypotheses of Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_314 are satisfied (each Z_i is closed integral of pure codimension j in X_{\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}}), and its conclusion, read with q \rightsquigarrow Q and m \rightsquigarrow r, gives for every i = 1,\dots,s
\[
F^{r}(\mathrm{cl}(Z_i)) \;=\; Q^{\,rj}\,\mathrm{cl}(Z_i) \;=\; (q^m)^{rj}\,\mathrm{cl}(Z_i) \;=\; q^{mrj}\,\mathrm{cl}(Z_i) \;=\; q^{m'j}\,\mathrm{cl}(Z_i),
\]
since mr = m'. Set c := q^{m'j} \in \mathbb Q_\ell^{\times} (a positive rational number, hence nonzero).

**Step 2 (all spanning vectors of W are eigenvectors of F^r for the single eigenvalue c).** By definition W is the \mathbb Q_\ell-span of the vectors F^t(\mathrm{cl}(Z_i)), 1 \le i \le s, t \ge 0. For each such generator, using that powers of F commute with each other and that F^t is \mathbb Q_\ell-linear (Step 0),
\[
F^{r}\bigl(F^{t}(\mathrm{cl}(Z_i))\bigr) = F^{t}\bigl(F^{r}(\mathrm{cl}(Z_i))\bigr) = F^{t}\bigl(c\,\mathrm{cl}(Z_i)\bigr) = c\,F^{t}(\mathrm{cl}(Z_i)),
\]
where the last equality uses c \in \mathbb Q_\ell and the \mathbb Q_\ell-linearity of F^t. Hence every vector of the chosen spanning set of W is an eigenvector of F^r with the common eigenvalue c.

**Step 3 (W is F-stable, and F|_W \in \mathrm{GL}(W)).** For each generator, F(F^t\mathrm{cl}(Z_i)) = F^{t+1}\mathrm{cl}(Z_i), which is again one of the spanning vectors of W; by \mathbb Q_\ell-linearity of F it follows that F(W) \subseteq W, which is the asserted F-stability. Since W is a \mathbb Q_\ell-subspace of the finite-dimensional space V, W is finite-dimensional; the restriction F|_W:W\to W is injective because F is an automorphism of V; an injective \mathbb Q_\ell-linear endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space is surjective, so F(W) = W and F|_W \in \mathrm{GL}(W). If W = 0 there is nothing to prove (F-stability is trivial and F|_W has no eigenvalues), so assume W \neq 0.

**Step 4 (apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_90).** Take V = W (finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell), T = F|_W \in \mathrm{GL}(W), the integer m of that lemma to be our r \ge 1, and c = q^{m'j} \in \mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}. Steps 2 and 3 verify its hypotheses: W is spanned by vectors v with T^r v = c v. Its conclusion yields
\[
(F|_W)^{r} = c\,\mathrm{id}_W = q^{m'j}\,\mathrm{id}_W,
\]
and (as a bonus, not needed here) that F|_W is semisimple.

**Step 5 (the eigenvalue computation).** Let \iota:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell \hookrightarrow \mathbb C be any embedding and let \alpha \in \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell be an eigenvalue of F|_W. The characteristic polynomial of F|_W lies in \mathbb Q_\ell[t], so its roots lie in \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, and Step 4 implies that the minimal polynomial of F|_W divides t^r - c; hence
\[
\alpha^{r} = c = q^{m'j}.
\]
Apply \iota. As \iota fixes the prime field \mathbb Q pointwise and c = q^{m'j} \in \mathbb Q, we get \iota(\alpha)^r = q^{m'j} \in \mathbb R_{>0}. Taking complex absolute values,
\[
|\iota(\alpha)|^{r} = \bigl|\iota(\alpha)^r\bigr| = q^{m'j}.
\]
Now |\iota(\alpha)| is a non-negative real number and q^{mj} is a positive real number with (q^{mj})^r = q^{mj\cdot r} = q^{m'j}; the positive real r-th root of a positive real number is unique, so
\[
|\iota(\alpha)| = q^{mj}.
\]
Finally, for any z \in \mathbb C one has z\bar z = |z|^2, therefore
\[
\iota(\alpha)\,\overline{\iota(\alpha)} = |\iota(\alpha)|^2 = \bigl(q^{mj}\bigr)^2 = q^{2mj},
\]
which is the desired identity.

**Conclusion.** W is an F-stable \mathbb Q_\ell-subspace of H^{2j}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), and for every embedding \iota:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C and every eigenvalue \alpha \in \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell of F|_W one has \iota(\alpha)\overline{\iota(\alpha)} = q^{2mj}. The case W = 0 was handled in Step 3 (vacuous eigenvalue statement, trivial stability). This completes the proof.

statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(K=\mathbb Q_\ell\), let \(L\) be a finite extension field of \(K\), and let \(\sigma\) be a \(K\)-algebra automorphism of \(L\) with \(\sigma^2=\mathrm{id}\). Suppose that for every \(K\)-embedding \(\tau:L\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\) and every \(z\in L\) one has \(\tau(\sigma(z))=\overline{\tau(z)}\). Then for every nonzero \(x\in L\), the element \(\operatorname{Tr}_{L/K}(x\,\sigma(x))\) of \(K\) is nonzero.
proof:
We prove the statement by pure field theory and the usual 'trace = sum of conjugates' formula; no geometric input is needed, and none of the listed lemmas is required.

NOTATION AND INTERPRETATION. Put n := [L:K] >= 1. Since K = Q_ell has characteristic 0, every extension of K is finite separable. A 'K-embedding tau: L -> C' is a field homomorphism tau: L -> C whose restriction to K equals a fixed reference embedding iota: K -> C (we identify K with iota(K) when convenient). Note first that the statement of the hypothesis is not vacuous and that iota is forced to have real image; both are shown below.

STEP 1 (Extension of iota to algebraic closures, and the count of K-embeddings into C).
Let Kbar be an algebraic closure of K containing L. The embedding iota: K -> C extends to a K-embedding iota_bar: Kbar -> C. Indeed, consider the set of pairs (E, j) with K <= E <= Kbar and j: E -> C a field homomorphism with j|_K = iota, ordered by extension; every chain has an upper bound given by the union of the fields and of the maps, so by Zorn's lemma there is a maximal element (E_max, j_max). If E_max were properly contained in Kbar, choose alpha in Kbar \ E_max and let P in E_max[t] be its minimal polynomial; since C is algebraically closed, P has a root beta in C (its image under j_max applied to the coefficients), and alpha |-> beta extends j_max to E_max(alpha), contradicting maximality. Hence E_max = Kbar.
Since char K = 0, L/K is separable, so |Emb_K(L, Kbar)| = [L:K] = n. Composition with iota_bar gives a map Emb_K(L, Kbar) -> Emb_K(L, C). It is injective. It is surjective: if tau: L -> C is a K-embedding, then every element of tau(L) is algebraic over iota(K), so tau(L) is contained in C^alg := {c in C : c algebraic over iota(K)}; and iota_bar(Kbar) is an algebraically closed algebraic extension of iota(K) inside C, hence equals C^alg (it is algebraic over iota(K), algebraically closed, and any element of C^alg is the image of some element of Kbar because Kbar is an algebraic closure of K and iota_bar maps Kbar onto an algebraically closed algebraic extension of iota(K), which must contain all elements of C algebraic over iota(K)). Thus iota_bar^{-1} o tau in Emb_K(L, Kbar) and tau is in the image. Consequently
  |Emb_K(L, C)| = n >= 1,
in particular Emb_K(L, C) is nonempty.

STEP 2 (The hypothesis forces iota(K) to be real; consistency check).
Emb_K(L, C) is nonempty by Step 1; fix tau_0 in Emb_K(L, C). For a in K, sigma(a) = a because sigma is a K-algebra automorphism, and tau_0(a) = iota(a). Applying the hypothesis with z = a gives iota(a) = tau_0(a) = tau_0(sigma(a)) = conjugate(tau_0(a)) = conjugate(iota(a)). Hence iota(K) is stable under complex conjugation, i.e. iota(K) subset R. (This is only a consistency check; it is not used further.)

STEP 3 (Trace formula).
For every y in L we claim
  iota_bar(Tr_{L/K}(y)) = sum_{tau in Emb_K(L, C)} tau(y).      (*)
Proof of the claim. Let m_y: L -> L, t |-> y t, be the K-linear multiplication map; by definition Tr_{L/K}(y) = Tr_K(m_y). Put F := K(y), f := [F:K], g := [L:F], so n = f g. Let P in K[t] be the minimal polynomial of y over K; then P is the characteristic polynomial of the F-linear map 'multiplication by y' on F (F = K(y) = K[y], and the matrix of multiplication by y in the F-basis {1} of F is the companion matrix of P). View L as an F-vector space of dimension g and choose an F-basis e_1, ..., e_g. The map m_y is F-linear (multiplication by y commutes with multiplication by elements of F), and its matrix over F in this basis is the same matrix as that of multiplication by y on F in the basis {1}. Choosing a K-basis of F and taking the corresponding K-basis {w_i e_j} of L, the matrix of m_y over K is block diagonal with g copies of that matrix. Hence
  chi_{m_y, L/K} = P^g,  so  Tr_{L/K}(y) = g * Tr_{F/K}(y) = g * (sum of the roots of P, with multiplicity).
Since char K = 0, P is separable: it has f distinct roots. The assignment sigma |-> sigma(y) is a bijection from Emb_K(F, Kbar) onto the set of roots of P in Kbar: it is injective because F = K(y), and surjective because a root alpha of P defines a K-isomorphism K(y) -> K(alpha), y |-> alpha, which is a K-embedding F -> Kbar. Writing Emb_K(F, Kbar) = {sigma_1, ..., sigma_f}, we obtain
  Tr_{L/K}(y) = g * sum_{i=1}^{f} sigma_i(y).                                    (1)
Each sigma_i extends to exactly g embeddings L -> Kbar over K: precomposing with sigma_i identifies these with Emb_F(L, Kbar), which has [L:F]_s = g elements because L/F is finite separable; and every element of Emb_K(L, Kbar) restricts to exactly one sigma_i. Therefore
  sum_{rho in Emb_K(L, Kbar)} rho(y) = sum_{i=1}^{f} g * sigma_i(y).             (2)
Combining (1) and (2) and applying iota_bar gives
  iota_bar(Tr_{L/K}(y)) = sum_{rho in Emb_K(L, Kbar)} iota_bar(rho(y)) = sum_{tau in Emb_K(L, C)} tau(y),
the last equality being the bijection of Step 1. This proves (*).

STEP 4 (Positivity for y = x sigma(x)).
Let 0 != x in L and set y := x sigma(x) in L. For any tau in Emb_K(L, C),
  tau(y) = tau(x) * tau(sigma(x)) = tau(x) * conjugate(tau(x)) = |tau(x)|^2,
where the middle equality is the hypothesis applied to z = x. The map tau is injective: its kernel is an ideal of the field L, and tau(1) = 1 != 0 in C, so ker tau = {0}. Since x != 0 we get tau(x) != 0, and therefore |tau(x)|^2 = tau(x) * conjugate(tau(x)) is a strictly positive real number. Summing (*) over the n = [L:K] embeddings,
  iota_bar(Tr_{L/K}(x sigma(x))) = sum_{tau in Emb_K(L, C)} |tau(x)|^2,
a finite sum of strictly positive real numbers; e.g. it is >= |tau_0(x)|^2 > 0 by Step 2. Hence
  iota_bar(Tr_{L/K}(x sigma(x))) != 0.

STEP 5 (Conclusion).
The element Tr_{L/K}(x sigma(x)) lies in K, and iota_bar|_K = iota is injective. From iota(Tr_{L/K}(x sigma(x))) != 0 we conclude Tr_{L/K}(x sigma(x)) != 0 in K, which is the desired conclusion. (In fact we proved the sharper statement that its image under iota is a strictly positive real number.)

EDGE CASES. If L = K then sigma = id (the only K-automorphism of K is the identity), Emb_K(L, C) = {iota}, and the argument gives iota(x^2) = |iota(x)|^2 > 0 for x != 0, so Tr_{K/K}(x sigma(x)) = x^2 != 0; this is covered by the general proof since n = 1 >= 1. The case x = 0 is excluded by hypothesis. The involution property sigma^2 = id is part of the standing hypotheses but is not needed in the argument: only the identities sigma|_K = id (used in Step 2, itself only a consistency check) and tau(sigma(x)) = conjugate(tau(x)) (used in Step 4) are used. All cases are thus exhausted, and the lemma is proved.

statement: Let \(Q=p^r\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, let \(A\) be an abelian variety over \(\mathbb F_Q\), let \(\pi\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)\) be the \(Q\)-power Frobenius endomorphism, and put \(V_\ell(A)=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(A)\). Then the multiset of eigenvalues of \(\pi\) acting on \(V_\ell(A)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), counted with algebraic multiplicity, is stable under \(\beta\mapsto Q\,\beta^{-1}\).
proof:
Proof. Let g = dim A. If g = 0, then V_l(A) = 0 by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_tate_rank, so the eigenvalue multiset is empty and is trivially stable. Assume g > 0.

First, V_l(A) is finite-dimensional over Q_l by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_tate_rank. The Q-power Frobenius pi is an F_Q-group homomorphism, because the group law of A is defined over F_Q and Frobenius commutes with polynomial maps over F_Q. It is an isogeny: it is finite (on affine opens Spec R the Frobenius map R -> R, f -> f^Q, makes R a finite module over its image, since R is of finite type over the perfect field F_Q) and it is surjective on geometric points (raising coordinates to the Q-th power is bijective on A(bar F_Q), as bar F_Q is algebraically closed). Since ell != p, eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_120 applies to the isogeny pi and shows that V_l(pi) is a Q_l-linear automorphism of V_l(A). Denote this automorphism again by pi.

Next choose an F_Q-rational polarization lambda of A. Such a polarization exists. By the definition of abelian variety used here, A is projective over F_Q, so a closed immersion A -> P^n_{F_Q} gives an ample invertible sheaf L = O(1)|_A defined over F_Q. For any line bundle L, the map lambda_L: A -> A^vee, x -> t_x^*L tensor L^{-1}, is a homomorphism defined over F_Q. If L is ample, lambda_L is an isogeny: its kernel is finite, since a positive-dimensional abelian subvariety B contained in the kernel would make L|_B translation invariant, and translation-invariant line bundles on an abelian variety lie in Pic^0 and are numerically trivial, contradicting ampleness of L|_B; and dim A = dim A^vee, so finite kernel implies the image has dimension g and is all of A^vee. Thus lambda_L is a polarization. Fix such a polarization lambda.

Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_104 with q = Q and m = 1. It gives a perfect alternating Q_l-bilinear pairing E_lambda: V_l(A) x V_l(A) -> Q_l(1) satisfying E_lambda(pi v, pi w) = Q E_lambda(v,w) for all v,w. Choose a nonzero element e in Q_l(1). Since Q_l(1) is one-dimensional over Q_l, every element of Q_l(1) can be written uniquely as a e. Define a Q_l-valued pairing <v,w> by E_lambda(v,w) = <v,w> e. Then < , > is perfect and bilinear, and <pi v, pi w> = Q <v,w>.

Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_113 to (A, lambda, pi, ell). It defines the adjoint u^* by E_lambda(uv,w) = E_lambda(v,u^*w) and proves pi^* = Q pi^{-1}. Under the identification of Q_l(1) with Q_l above, this adjoint is exactly the adjoint u^dagger for the pairing < , >, because <uv,w> = <v,u^dagger w> is equivalent to E_lambda(uv,w) = E_lambda(v,u^dagger w). Hence T = pi and c = Q satisfy T^dagger = c T^{-1} with respect to the perfect pairing < , >. Note that c = Q lies in Q_l^* because ell != p.

Now apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_69 to V = V_l(A), T = pi, c = Q, and the pairing < , >. Part (3) of lemma_69 says that if alpha_1,...,alpha_N in Qbar_l^* are the eigenvalues of T on V tensor Qbar_l counted with algebraic multiplicity, then the multisets {alpha_1,...,alpha_N} and {c/alpha_1,...,c/alpha_N} coincide. The nonzero condition is automatic because T is invertible. Taking c = Q gives that the eigenvalue multiset of pi is stable under beta -> Q beta^{-1}. No semisimplicity assumption is used.

Thus the multiset of eigenvalues of pi on V_l(A) tensor Qbar_l, counted with algebraic multiplicity, is stable under beta -> Q beta^{-1}.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge2\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and \(Y\subsetneq X\) a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\), with closed immersion \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); let \(\xi=\mathrm{cl}(Y)\), let \(L\) and \(L_Y\) be cup product with \(\xi\) and with \(i^*\xi\), let \(\operatorname{tr}_Y\) be the Poincar\'e duality trace on \(Y\) normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_Y(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^m}]\), and set \(\beta^Y(u,v)=\operatorname{tr}_Y(u\cup v)\) on \(H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Let \(F\) be the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius. Suppose every \(F\)-stable \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-subspace \(W\subseteq\ker(L_Y:H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell))\) on which \(\beta^Y\) vanishes identically is zero. Then \(L:H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is injective.
proof:
Write $H^n(X):=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $H^n(Y):=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, and write $F_X,F_Y$ for the $q^m$-power arithmetic Frobenius $(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}$, on $H^*(X)$ and $H^*(Y)$; the $F$ of the statement is these maps. Put
\[
K:=\ker\bigl(L:H^{d-1}(X)\to H^{d+1}(X)\bigr),\qquad W:=\operatorname{im}\bigl(i^*:H^{d-1}(X)\to H^{d-1}(Y)\bigr).
\]
We must prove $K=0$.

**Step 0: The geometric input applies.** Since $X$ is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $d\ge2$ over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, $X_k$ is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $d$ over the algebraically closed field $k$. Since $Y$ is smooth of pure dimension $d-1\ge1$ over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$ it is nonempty, and the (faithfully flat, hence surjective) projection $Y_k\to Y$ shows $Y_k\neq\varnothing$; $Y_k$ is smooth of pure dimension $d-1$ over $k$, and $Y_k\subsetneq X_k$ because $Y\subsetneq X$. Being very ample, $Y$ is an ample Cartier divisor, and ampleness and effectivity are preserved by the base change $k/\mathbb F_{q^m}$. Thus $Y_k\subsetneq X_k$ is a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor, smooth of pure dimension $d-1$, as required in Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_420 and in Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/5e8133.

**Step 1: $i^*$ is injective in degree $d-1$.** By Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_420 applied to $X_k$ and $Y_k$, the pullback $i^*:H^m(X)\to H^m(Y)$ is injective for $m=d-1$. Hence for every subspace $U\subseteq H^{d-1}(X)$, $i^*(U)=0$ implies $U=0$. In particular $K=0$ will follow once we show $i^*(K)=0$.

**Step 2: $i^*$ is $F$-equivariant.** The morphism $i:Y\hookrightarrow X$ is defined over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, so $i_k\circ(\mathrm{id}_{Y_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)\circ i_k$ as morphisms $Y_k\to X_k$ (both are the morphism obtained from $i$ and the identity on $\operatorname{Spec}\sigma$ on the base). Contravariance of pullback gives $i^*\circ F_X=F_Y\circ i^*$ on $H^*(X)$.

**Step 3: $F$ scales $\xi$, and $K$ is $F$-stable.** The divisor $Y$ is an effective codimension-$1$ cycle on $X$ defined over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$ and $\xi=\mathrm{cl}(Y)$. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_587 (with $j=1$ and $q$ replaced by $q^m$), $F_X(\xi)=q^{-m}\xi$. Since $F_X$ is a ring automorphism for the cup product,
\[
F_X(Lx)=F_X(\xi\cup x)=F_X(\xi)\cup F_X(x)=q^{-m}\,\bigl(\xi\cup F_X(x)\bigr)=q^{-m}L(F_X x)\qquad(x\in H^{d-1}(X)).
\]
As $q^{-m}\neq0$ and $F_X$ is invertible, $x\in K\iff Lx=0\iff F_X(Lx)=0\iff L(F_Xx)=0\iff F_Xx\in K$. Thus $F_X(K)=K$; in particular $K$ is an $F$-stable $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspace of $H^{d-1}(X)$.

**Step 4: $i^*(K)\subseteq\ker L_Y$.** Let $x\in K$. Using functoriality of the cup product with respect to pullback and $L_Y=\xi_Y\cup(-)$ with $\xi_Y=i^*\xi$,
\[
L_Y(i^*x)=(i^*\xi)\cup(i^*x)=i^*(\xi\cup x)=i^*(Lx)=i^*(0)=0.
\]
Hence $i^*(K)\subseteq\ker\bigl(L_Y:H^{d-1}(Y)\to H^{d+1}(Y)\bigr)$.

**Step 5: $i^*(K)$ is $F$-stable.** By Step 2 and Step 3, $F_Y(i^*(K))=i^*(F_XK)=i^*(K)$. Together with Step 4, $i^*(K)$ is an $F$-stable $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspace of $\ker L_Y$.

**Step 6: $\beta^Y$ vanishes identically on $i^*(K)$.** Apply Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/5e8133 to $X_k$, $Y_k$, $\xi$ and $\operatorname{tr}_Y$: the map $i^*$ induces an isomorphism
\[
i^*|_K:\;K\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\{\,w\in W\mid \operatorname{tr}_Y(w\cup v)=0\ \text{for every } v\in W\,\}.
\]
Consequently, for every $u\in i^*(K)$ one has $\operatorname{tr}_Y(u\cup v)=0$ for all $v\in W$. Since $i^*(K)\subseteq W$ by definition of $W$, taking $v\in i^*(K)$ gives $\beta^Y(u,v)=\operatorname{tr}_Y(u\cup v)=0$ for all $u,v\in i^*(K)$; that is, $\beta^Y$ vanishes identically on $i^*(K)$. (This vanishing statement is independent of the normalisation of $\operatorname{tr}_Y$: the trace of the statement is the Poincar\'e duality trace with $\operatorname{tr}_Y(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^m}]$, and any two such choices differ by a nonzero scalar, which does not affect the condition $\operatorname{tr}_Y(w\cup v)=0$.)

**Step 7: Conclusion.** By the hypothesis of the lemma, every $F$-stable $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspace of $\ker L_Y$ on which $\beta^Y$ vanishes identically is zero. Steps 4, 5 and 6 show that $i^*(K)$ is such a subspace, so $i^*(K)=0$. By the injectivity of $i^*$ on $H^{d-1}(X)$ (Step 1), $K=0$. Therefore $L:H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is injective, which is the desired conclusion.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\); fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle class of an \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-rational very ample divisor, let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\), let \(\operatorname{tr}_X:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) be the Poincar\'e duality trace normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_X(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^m}]\), put \(\beta_0(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(L^{d}x\cup y)\) for \(x,y\in H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), and let \(F\) be the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius. Setting \(G_0(x,y)=\beta_0(x,Fy)+\beta_0(x,F^{-1}y)\), one has \(G_0(x,x)\neq0\) for every nonzero \(x\in H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
proof:
We write $K=\mathbb F_{q^m}$ and $F=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}$, for the $q^m$-power arithmetic Frobenius. By lemma_6a, $F$ is an invertible $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear operator on each $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, so $F^{-1}$ on $H^0$ is well defined.

**Step 1: $H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell\cdot 1$ and $F|_{H^0}=\mathrm{id}$.** Since $X$ is geometrically connected over $K$, the fibre $X_k$ is connected; it is noetherian, so its \'etale topos is connected and the global sections of any constant sheaf $A$ on $X_{k,\mathrm{\acute et}}$ are just $A$. Hence $H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Z/\ell^n)\cong\mathbb Z/\ell^n$ for every $n$, and therefore $H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell):=(\varprojlim_n H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Z/\ell^n))\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell\cong\mathbb Z_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell=\mathbb Q_\ell$, generated by the unit class $1$.

The operator $F$ is the pullback along the morphism of topoi induced by $(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)$; pullback of sheaves is symmetric monoidal and carries the constant sheaf to the constant sheaf, so $F$ is a homomorphism of graded $\mathbb Q_\ell$-algebras preserving the unit: $F(1)=1$. Being $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear (lemma_6a) and acting on the $1$-dimensional space $\mathbb Q_\ell\cdot 1$, it follows that $F(\lambda\cdot 1)=\lambda\cdot 1$ for all $\lambda\in\mathbb Q_\ell$, i.e. $F|_{H^0}=\mathrm{id}$, and hence also $F^{-1}|_{H^0}=\mathrm{id}$.

**Step 2: The trace $\operatorname{tr}_X$ coincides with the degree map of lemma_247.** Fix the given nonzero element $\tau\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ and use it to identify $\mathbb Q_\ell(d)\simeq\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\simeq\mathbb Q_\ell$. Let $f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}K$ be the structure morphism and let $\deg_X:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(d))\to\mathbb Q_\ell$ be the degree map of lemma_247, characterised by $\deg_X(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):K]$ for every closed point $z\in X$. By lemma_77(a) the Poincar\'e duality trace $\operatorname{tr}:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ is likewise characterised by $\operatorname{tr}(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):K]$; this is exactly the $\operatorname{tr}_X$ of the statement.

By lemma_77(b) the pairing $H^0\times H^{2d}\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$, $(x,y)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup y)$, is perfect, so $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^0=1$. For any closed point $z$, $\operatorname{tr}_X(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):K]\neq 0$, so $\mathrm{cl}(z)$ is a basis of $H^{2d}$. After the twist identifications, both $\deg_X$ and $\operatorname{tr}_X$ are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear functionals on the $1$-dimensional space $H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ taking the same nonzero value $[\kappa(z):K]$ on the basis element $\mathrm{cl}(z)$; hence they coincide:
$$\deg_X(u)=\operatorname{tr}_X(u)\qquad\text{for all }u\in H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\ (\text{under }\mathbb Q_\ell(d)\simeq\mathbb Q_\ell).\tag{$*$}$$

**Step 3: $\operatorname{tr}_X(\xi^d)$ is a positive integer.** Let $H$ be the $K$-rational very ample divisor whose cycle class is $\xi$, and put $\mathcal L=\mathcal O_X(H)$, an ample line bundle defined over $K$. Its first Chern class $c_1(\mathcal L)\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))$ corresponds, under $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\simeq\mathbb Q_\ell$, to the cycle class $\xi$ of $H$.

Apply lemma_247 (over the base field $K=\mathbb F_{q^m}$) to $f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}K$: here $D=d$, $E=0$, $r=d$, and $\operatorname{Spec}K$ is smooth, projective and geometrically connected of pure dimension $0$ over $K$. The lemma gives a positive integer $N$ such that
$$\deg_X\!\bigl(c_1(\mathcal L)^{d}\cup f^*u\bigr)=N\,\deg_{\operatorname{Spec}K}(u)\quad\text{for every }u\in H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((\operatorname{Spec}K)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(0)).$$
Take $u=1$. Then $f^*(1)=1$, and $\deg_{\operatorname{Spec}K}(1)=[\kappa(z_0):K]=1$ for the unique closed point $z_0$ of $\operatorname{Spec}K$. Hence
$$\deg_X\bigl(c_1(\mathcal L)^{d}\bigr)=N\in\mathbb Z_{>0}.$$
Using $(*)$ and the identification of $c_1(\mathcal L)^d$ with $\xi^d$, we obtain
$$\operatorname{tr}_X(\xi^d)=N\in\mathbb Q_\ell,\qquad N\ge 1.$$
In particular $\operatorname{tr}_X(\xi^d)\neq 0$ (its image in $\mathbb Q_\ell$ is the nonzero element $N$).

(Concretely, $N=\deg_H(X)>0$ is the degree of the $0$-dimensional proper intersection of $d$ general members of $|H|$; lemma_247 is the formal input that the $\ell$-adic number $\operatorname{tr}_X(\xi^d)$ is this positive integer.)

**Step 4: Evaluation of $\beta_0$ and $G_0$ on $H^0$.** Let $x\in H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ be nonzero; write $x=\lambda\cdot 1$ with $\lambda\in\mathbb Q_\ell^\times$. Since $H^0$ is concentrated in degree $0$, cup product on it is commutative with no sign, and $L^d x\cup y=x\cup y\cup\xi^d$. For $x=\lambda\cdot1$, $y=\mu\cdot1$,
$$\beta_0(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl((\lambda\mu)\,\xi^d\bigr)=\lambda\mu\,\operatorname{tr}_X(\xi^d)=\lambda\mu\,N.$$
By Step 1, $F(x)=x$ and $F^{-1}(x)=x$. Therefore
$$G_0(x,x)=\beta_0(x,Fx)+\beta_0(x,F^{-1}x)=\beta_0(x,x)+\beta_0(x,x)=2\lambda^2 N.$$

**Step 5: Non-vanishing.** $\mathbb Q_\ell$ is a field of characteristic $0$, so $2\neq 0$; $\lambda\neq 0$ by assumption, so $\lambda^2\neq 0$; and $N\ge 1$ is a nonzero element of $\mathbb Q_\ell$. Hence $G_0(x,x)=2\lambda^2N\neq 0$ in $\mathbb Q_\ell$.

This holds for every nonzero $x\in H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, which is the claim. (No hypothesis on $d\ge 2$ was used: for $d=1$ the same argument reads $\operatorname{tr}_X(\xi)=\deg H>0$, which is the case $r=1$ of lemma_247 with $f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}K$.)

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge2\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and \(Y\subsetneq X\) a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\), with closed immersion \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); let \(\xi=\mathrm{cl}(Y)\), let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\), let \(L_Y\) be cup product with \(i^*\xi\), let \(\operatorname{tr}_Y:H^{2d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) be the Poincar\'e duality trace normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_Y(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^m}]\), and put \(\beta^Y(u,v)=\operatorname{tr}_Y(u\cup v)\) for \(u,v\in H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Let \(F\) be the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius and \(K=i^*\bigl(\ker(L:H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell))\bigr)\). Then \(K\) is an \(F\)-stable \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-subspace of \(\ker(L_Y:H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell))\) on which \(\beta^Y\) vanishes identically.
proof:
{
"lemma_id": "Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/9efee7",
"cited_lemmas": ["eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_291", "eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_439_gysin_projection_formula_divisor", "eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77"],
"cited_references": [],
"proof": "Write $K_0=\mathbb F_{q^m}$ (a prime power $q^m=p^{ma}$), $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, and $\sigma:k\to k$, $c\mapsto c^{q^m}$. For $Z\in\{X,Y\}$ put $F_Z:=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$, the $q^m$-power arithmetic Frobenius of $H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$; we write $F$ for both when no confusion is possible. All Tate twists are identified with $\mathbb Q_\ell$ using the single fixed nonzero element of $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ supplied by the statement, and $\xi=\mathrm{cl}(Y)\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is the cycle class of $Y$ under this identification.

=== Step 0. Functoriality facts that will be used repeatedly ===

(0.1) For each $Z$, $H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is a graded-commutative $\mathbb Q_\ell$-algebra (étale cohomology of the constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$, which is a sheaf of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-algebras), and pullback along any morphism of $k$-schemes is a homomorphism of graded $\mathbb Q_\ell$-algebras preserving the unit. In particular both $F_Z$ and $i^*$ are graded $\mathbb Q_\ell$-algebra homomorphisms, so for all classes $a,b$ of the right degrees,
\[ F(a\cup b)=Fa\cup Fb,\qquad i^*(a\cup b)=i^*a\cup i^*b, \]
and $F(1)=1$, $i^*(1)=1$.

(0.2) The square
\[ \begin{CD} Y_k @>{F_Y}>> Y_k\\ @V{i_k}VV @VV{i_k}V\\ X_k @>{F_X}>> X_k \end{CD} \]
commutes. Indeed $i_k=i\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Spec}\,k}$ and $F_Z=\mathrm{id}_{Z}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma$; since $i:Y\hookrightarrow X$ is a morphism over $K_0=\mathbb F_{q^m}$, both composites $Y_k\to X_k$ are the morphism induced on the fibre product $Y\times_{\mathrm{Spec}\,K_0}\mathrm{Spec}\,k$ by the pair $(i,\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Spec}\,k})$ (the two ways of forming this pair agree because $i$ is $K_0$-linear, so the induced maps to $\mathrm{Spec}\,K_0$ coincide). Hence by contravariance
\[ i^*\circ F_X=F_Y\circ i^* \tag{0.2a}\]
on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $n$.

(0.3) The trace. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77 applied to the smooth projective geometrically connected $K_0$-scheme $Y$ of pure dimension $d-1$, the cycle-class/Gysin isomorphism gives a trace $\mathrm{tr}:H^{2d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-(d-1))$ which, after the fixed identification $\mathbb Q_\ell(d-1)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell$, satisfies $\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^m}]$ for every closed point $z$ of $Y$, and for which the pairing $H^n(Y_k)\times H^{2d-2-n}(Y_k)\to\mathbb Q_\ell$, $(u,v)\mapsto\mathrm{tr}(u\cup v)$, is perfect. Taking $n=0$ and using that $Y$ is geometrically connected, so $H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell$ is one-dimensional generated by $1$, perfectness forces $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^{2d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=1$. Since a closed point $z$ has $\mathrm{cl}(z)\neq0$ (its trace is $[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^m}]>0$), $\mathrm{cl}(z)$ spans $H^{2d-2}(Y_k)$, so the normalisation condition $\mathrm{tr}_Y(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^m}]$ determines $\mathrm{tr}_Y$ uniquely. Therefore the map $\mathrm{tr}_Y$ of the statement is exactly the trace supplied by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77 (and hence exactly the trace used in eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_439_gysin_projection_formula_divisor, whose $Y$-trace is the sum of the traces on the connected components of $Y_k$, here just the single component $Y_k$). In particular $\beta^Y(u,v)=\mathrm{tr}_Y(u\cup v)$ is a well-defined $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinear form on $H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, since $u\cup v\in H^{2d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ where $\mathrm{tr}_Y$ lives.

=== Step 1. Frobenius on $\xi$ ===

Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_291 with its prime power $q$ replaced by $q^m=p^{ma}$, with its variety $X$ equal to our $X$ (smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $d$ over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$), with its parameter $m$ equal to $1$ (our cycle $Y$ is defined over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$ itself), and with $j=1$ (the cycle $Y$ has codimension $1$). Its conclusion, with $F$ the $q^m$-power arithmetic Frobenius, is
\[ F(\mathrm{cl}(Y))=(q^m)^{1\cdot 1}\,\mathrm{cl}(Y)=q^m\,\xi, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad F_X\xi=q^m\xi. \tag{1.1}\]
Since $F_X$ is an automorphism, (1.1) is equivalent to
\[ F_X^{-1}\xi=q^{-m}\xi. \tag{1.2}\]
Combining (1.1) with (0.2a) gives also
\[ F_Y(i^*\xi)=i^*(F_X\xi)=i^*(q^m\xi)=q^m\,i^*\xi. \tag{1.3}\]

=== Step 2. The Gysin map and the class $\xi$ ===

We invoke eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_439_gysin_projection_formula_divisor, with its $q$ replaced by $q^m$. Its hypotheses are satisfied: $X$ is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $d\ge2\ge1$ over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, $Y\subsetneq X$ is a smooth effective divisor of pure dimension $d-1$ defined over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$ (a fortiori, being a smooth geometrically connected very ample Cartier divisor), $\ell\ne p$, and the identification of twists is the fixed one. That lemma provides, for every $n\ge0$, the Gysin homomorphism
\[ i_!:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^{n+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \]
characterised by
\[ \mathrm{tr}_X(i_!a\cup b)=\mathrm{tr}_Y(a\cup i^*b)\quad\text{for all }a\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\ b\in H^{2d-2-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), \tag{2.1}\]
where $\mathrm{tr}_X$ is the similarly normalised trace on $X$ ($\mathrm{tr}_X(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^m}]$), and it proves the projection formula
\[ i_!(i^*x)=x\cup\xi\quad\text{for all }x\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\ n\ge0. \tag{2.2}\]
(The $\mathrm{tr}_Y$ appearing in (2.1) is the one of Step 0.3, by the uniqueness proved there.)

Taking $n=0$ and $x=1\in H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ in (2.2), and using $i^*(1)=1$ and $1\cup\xi=\xi$, we obtain
\[ i_!(1)=\xi. \tag{2.3}\]

=== Step 3. The key trace identity ===

Let $\gamma\in H^{2d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ be arbitrary. Apply the characterising property (2.1) with $n=0$, $a=1\in H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $b=\gamma$ (note $2d-2-0=2d-2$, so $b$ is in the required degree). Then
\[ \mathrm{tr}_X(i_!1\cup\gamma)=\mathrm{tr}_Y(1\cup i^*\gamma)=\mathrm{tr}_Y(i^*\gamma), \]
the last equality because $1$ is the unit of the cohomology ring of $Y_k$. Using (2.3) we conclude
\[ \mathrm{tr}_Y(i^*\gamma)=\mathrm{tr}_X(\xi\cup\gamma)\qquad\text{for all }\gamma\in H^{2d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). \tag{3.1}\]

=== Step 4. $K$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspace ===

$\ker\bigl(L:H^{d-1}(X_k)\to H^{d+1}(X_k)\bigr)$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspace because $L$, being cup product with the fixed class $\xi$, is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear. The pullback $i^*:H^{d-1}(X_k)\to H^{d-1}(Y_k)$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear, so its image of a subspace is a subspace:
\[ K=i^*\bigl(\ker L\bigr)\subseteq H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\ \text{ is a }\mathbb Q_\ell\text{-subspace.}\]

=== Step 5. $K\subseteq\ker L_Y$ ===

Let $u\in K$, say $u=i^*x$ with $x\in\ker L$, i.e. $Lx=\xi\cup x=0$. Then, using that $i^*$ is a ring homomorphism,
\[ L_Y(u)=i^*\xi\cup u=i^*\xi\cup i^*x=i^*(\xi\cup x)=i^*(Lx)=i^*(0)=0. \]
Hence $u\in\ker\bigl(L_Y:H^{d-1}(Y_k)\to H^{d+1}(Y_k)\bigr)$, and as $u$ was arbitrary, $K\subseteq\ker L_Y$. (No assumption on $d$ is needed: when $d=2$ one has $H^3(Y_k)=0$ by vanishing above twice the dimension, so the claim is then automatic anyway; the argument above covers every $d\ge2$ uniformly.)

=== Step 6. $K$ is $F$-stable ===

Let $u\in K$, $u=i^*x$ with $Lx=0$. Using (0.2a),
\[ F_Yu=F_Y(i^*x)=i^*(F_Xx). \]
We first check that $\xi\cup F_Xx=0$. By (1.2) and the fact that $F_X$ is a ring homomorphism,
\[ \xi\cup F_Xx=F_X\bigl(F_X^{-1}\xi\bigr)\cup F_Xx=F_X\bigl(F_X^{-1}\xi\cup x\bigr)=F_X\bigl(q^{-m}\xi\cup x\bigr)=q^{-m}F_X(\xi\cup x)=q^{-m}F_X(Lx)=0, \]
where each use of $F_X$ as a ring homomorphism is legitimate since $F_X^{-1}\xi\in H^2$ and $x\in H^{d-1}$. Therefore, using again that $i^*$ is a ring homomorphism,
\[ L_Y(F_Yu)=i^*\xi\cup F_Yu=i^*\xi\cup i^*(F_Xx)=i^*(\xi\cup F_Xx)=i^*(0)=0, \]
so $F_Yu\in\ker L_Y$, and moreover $F_Yu=i^*(F_Xx)$ exhibits it as the $i^*$-image of an element of $\ker L$, hence $F_Yu\in K$. Thus $F_Y(K)\subseteq K$; since $F_Y$ is an automorphism and $K$ is finite-dimensional, $F_Y|_K$ is an automorphism of $K$. So $K$ is $F$-stable.

=== Step 7. $\beta^Y$ vanishes identically on $K\times K$ ===

Let $u,v\in K$, say $u=i^*x$ and $v=i^*y$ with $x,y\in\ker L\subseteq H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Then $x\cup y\in H^{2d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, so we may apply (3.1) with $\gamma=x\cup y$:
\[ \beta^Y(u,v)=\mathrm{tr}_Y(u\cup v)=\mathrm{tr}_Y(i^*x\cup i^*y)=\mathrm{tr}_Y\bigl(i^*(x\cup y)\bigr)=\mathrm{tr}_X\bigl(\xi\cup x\cup y\bigr). \]
By graded commutativity and associativity of the cup product, $\xi\cup x\cup y=(\xi\cup x)\cup y=(Lx)\cup y=0\cup y=0$, because $x\in\ker L$. Hence
\[ \beta^Y(u,v)=\mathrm{tr}_X(0)=0. \]
As $u,v\in K$ were arbitrary, $\beta^Y$ vanishes identically on $K\times K$.

=== Conclusion ===

Steps 4, 5, 6 and 7 together say exactly that $K=i^*\bigl(\ker(L:H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell))\bigr)$ is an $F$-stable $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspace of $\ker\bigl(L_Y:H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)$ on which $\beta^Y$ vanishes identically. This completes the proof. 

(Remark on the role of very ampleness: the argument used only that $Y$ is a nonempty effective Cartier divisor over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension $d-1$, so that the Gysin formalism of eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_439_gysin_projection_formula_divisor and the cycle-class Frobenius computation of eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_291 apply; very ampleness is more than needed here.)
}

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(m\ge1\), let \(V\) be a nonzero finite-dimensional vector space over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and let \(\Omega\) be a nonempty open subscheme of the projective space \(\mathbb P(V)\) defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Then there exist an integer \(r\ge1\) divisible by \(m\) and a point of \(\Omega(\mathbb F_{q^r})\).
proof:
Proof.
Let k = F_{q^m}. Choose a k-basis of V and identify P(V) with P^d_k, where d = dim_k V - 1. Write Omega for the corresponding open subscheme.

If Omega = P^d_k, then the coordinate point [1:0:...:0] is a k-rational point. Taking r = m gives a point of Omega(F_{q^r}).

Assume now that Omega != P^d_k. Choose a point y in Omega. Let S = k[X_0,...,X_d] be the homogeneous coordinate ring of P^d_k. By the definition of the Zariski topology on Proj(S), the sets D_+(F), where F ranges over nonzero homogeneous elements of S, form a basis of open subsets. Hence there exists a nonzero homogeneous F in S such that y lies in D_+(F) and D_+(F) is contained in Omega.

We claim that there exist a finite extension K/k and a point x in P^d(K) with F(x) != 0. Let kbar be an algebraic closure of k. The field kbar is infinite: for every n >= 1, the polynomial T^{q^n} - T has q^n distinct roots in kbar.

We use the elementary fact that a nonzero polynomial over an infinite field is not the zero function. For completeness, prove it by induction on the number n of variables. If n = 1, a nonzero polynomial has at most deg(p) zeros, so it cannot vanish on all of the infinite field. If n > 1, write the polynomial as sum_{j=0}^N g_j(x_1,...,x_{n-1}) x_n^j. Choose j with g_j nonzero. By the induction hypothesis choose (a_1,...,a_{n-1}) such that g_j(a_1,...,a_{n-1}) != 0. Then the one-variable polynomial sum_{j=0}^N g_j(a_1,...,a_{n-1}) t^j is nonzero, so by the n = 1 case there is a_n with this polynomial nonzero at a_n. Thus the original polynomial is nonzero at (a_1,...,a_{n-1},a_n).

Apply this fact to F as a polynomial over kbar. There exists b = (b_0,...,b_d) in kbar^{d+1} such that F(b) != 0. If deg F > 0, then F(0,...,0) = 0, so b is automatically nonzero. If deg F = 0, then F is a nonzero constant and we may take b = (1,0,...,0) over k. Put K = k(b_0,...,b_d). Since each b_i is algebraic over the finite field k, K is generated over k by finitely many algebraic elements, hence K/k is a finite extension. Therefore K is a finite field.

Let r = [K : F_q]. Since k = F_{q^m} is contained in K, the tower law gives r = [K : k] [k : F_q] = [K : k] m. Thus m divides r, and K is isomorphic to F_{q^r}. The nonzero vector b defines a K-rational point x = [b_0:...:b_d] of P^d_k. Because F(b) != 0, this point lies in D_+(F). Since D_+(F) is contained in Omega, x factors through Omega. Hence x is a point of Omega(K) = Omega(F_{q^r}).

This completes the proof.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge2\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(Y\subsetneq X\) be a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) that is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and let \(j:U=X\setminus Y\hookrightarrow X\) be the open complement. Then \(H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell):=H^j(X_k,j_!\mathbb Q_\ell)\) vanishes for every integer \(j>2d\).
proof:
We prove that H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=H^j(X_k,(j_k)_!\mathbb Q_\ell)=0 for every integer j>2d, where j_k:U_k\hookrightarrow X_k is the base change of j. No Frobenius-semisimplicity input is needed; the argument is purely the localisation long exact sequence plus the vanishing of projective cohomology above twice the dimension.

Step 1: The geometric situation over k. Put Q:=q^m=p^{am}, which is again a prime power, and let K_0:=\mathbb F_{q^m}=\mathbb F_Q. By hypothesis X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d\ge 2 over K_0, and Y\subsetneq X is a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor, defined over K_0, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d-1 over K_0. Since Y is an effective Cartier divisor and Y\subsetneq X, Y is a proper closed subscheme, and its base change Y_k\to X_k is again a closed immersion (closed immersions are stable under base change). The open complement of Y_k in X_k is (X\setminus Y)_k=U_k, because taking the open complement commutes with base change. Hence the base-changed open immersion j_k:U_k\hookrightarrow X_k is exactly the complement of the closed immersion i_k:Y_k\hookrightarrow X_k, and the sheaf (j_k)_!\mathbb Q_\ell appearing in the statement is the extension by zero of the constant sheaf along that open immersion of (X_k)_{\mathrm{\acute et}}.

The field k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q=\overline{\mathbb F_{q^m}} is algebraically closed of characteristic p, and \ell\neq p. Since X is smooth of relative dimension d over K_0, X_k is smooth of relative dimension d over k, hence regular; a regular scheme has open irreducible components, so a connected regular scheme is integral, and X_k is connected because X is geometrically connected. Thus X_k is an integral (in particular a projective) k-scheme of pure dimension d. The same reasoning applied to Y, which is smooth of relative dimension d-1 over K_0 and geometrically connected, shows that Y_k is a projective k-scheme of pure dimension d-1 (and d-1\ge 1\ge 0).

Step 2: The localisation long exact sequence. Apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_283 with the prime power Q=q^m in place of its q, with X, Y, U, j, i as above, and with k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q=\overline{\mathbb F_Q} (note that all its hypotheses hold by Step 1: X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d\ge 1 over \mathbb F_Q, and Y is an effective ample divisor over \mathbb F_Q, smooth of pure dimension d-1). It yields a long exact sequence of finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces
\[\cdots\to H^{n}_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{i_k^*}H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\delta_n}H^{n+1}_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{n+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to\cdots\]
In this sequence H^n_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is precisely H^n((X_k)_{\mathrm{\acute et}},(j_k)_!\mathbb Q_\ell): this is the definition of compactly supported cohomology used in Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_localization_les_finite_type, which is the geometric form of the same sequence for the complementary pair (Y_k\subset X_k, U_k\subset X_k) of Step 1, and it coincides with the notation H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) of the statement. (The Frobenius equivariance of the maps supplied by lemma_283 is not needed here.)

Step 3: Vanishing of the outer terms for degrees above 2d. Let j>2d be an integer; then j\ge 2d+1.

(a) For X_k: it is a projective scheme over the algebraically closed field k of pure dimension d, and \ell\neq\mathrm{char}(k). By Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing (applied with d\rightsquigarrow d and n\rightsquigarrow j), H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0 for every m>2d; in particular
\[H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0.\]

(b) For Y_k: it is a projective scheme over k of pure dimension d-1, so the same lemma applied with d\rightsquigarrow d-1 gives H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0 for every m>2(d-1)=2d-2. Since j\ge 2d+1 we have j-1\ge 2d>2d-2, hence
\[H^{j-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0.\]

Step 4: Exactness forces the middle term to vanish. Take the segment of the long exact sequence of Step 2 with n:=j-1 (note j-1\ge 2d\ge 4\ge 0, so this is an ordinary segment of the sequence, no negative-degree convention is involved):
\[H^{j-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^{j-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\delta_{j-1}}H^{j}_{c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^{j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).\]
By Step 3(b) the left-hand outer term H^{j-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is the zero vector space, so \mathrm{im}(\delta_{j-1})=0; equivalently \ker\bigl(H^{j}_{c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)=\mathrm{im}(\delta_{j-1})=0 by exactness at H^j_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). By Step 3(a) the right-hand term H^{j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is also zero, so the map H^{j}_{c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to 0 has kernel all of H^{j}_{c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). Combining, H^{j}_{c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0.

Step 5: Conclusion. Since j>2d was arbitrary, H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=H^j(X_k,(j_k)_!\mathbb Q_\ell)=0 for every integer j>2d, which is exactly the claimed statement. No assertion is made (nor needed) in degrees j\le 2d; indeed H^d_{c} and H^{2d}_{c} are in general nonzero (e.g. X=\mathbb P^2, Y a hyperplane gives U=\mathbb A^2 with H^4_c\neq 0), so the bound j>2d is the correct upper end of the range.

(Remark on base change: all groups in the argument are computed on the geometric fibres X_k, Y_k, U_k, so passing from the ground field \mathbb F_{q^m} to k involves no cohomological base-change theorem; only the elementary facts that closed immersions, open complements and smoothness are preserved by base change, used in Step 1.)

statement: Let ℓ be a prime, let A and B be graded Q_ℓ-algebras, let α∈A^2 and β∈B^2, let c∈Q_ℓ^×, and let φ:A→B be an isomorphism of graded Q_ℓ-algebras such that φ(α)=cβ. Suppose that for an integer d≥0 and for every n with 0≤n≤d the map A^n→A^{2d−n}, x↦α^{d−n}x, is an isomorphism. Then for every n with 0≤n≤d the map B^n→B^{2d−n}, y↦β^{d−n}y, is an isomorphism.
proof:
We prove the statement purely algebraically; no geometry is involved. Write A = \bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z} A^n and B = \bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z} B^n for the given graded \mathbb Q_\ell-algebras (unital, with the structure map \mathbb Q_\ell \to A (resp. B) sending the base field into the centre), with \alpha\in A^2, \beta\in B^2, c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}, and \varphi:A\xrightarrow{\sim} B an isomorphism of graded \mathbb Q_\ell-algebras satisfying \varphi(\alpha)=c\beta. Fix an integer d\ge 0 and assume that for every n with 0\le n\le d the map
\[\lambda_A(n):A^n\longrightarrow A^{2d-n},\qquad x\longmapsto \alpha^{\,d-n}x\]
is an isomorphism of \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces. We must show that for every such n the map
\[\lambda_B(n):B^n\longrightarrow B^{2d-n},\qquad y\longmapsto \beta^{\,d-n}y\]
is an isomorphism.

Step 1 (the maps are well defined and \mathbb Q_\ell-linear). Since \alpha\in A^2, we have \alpha^{m}\in A^{2m} for every m\ge 0 (products of homogeneous elements are homogeneous of the sum of the degrees), so for x\in A^n, \alpha^{d-n}x\in A^{2(d-n)+n}=A^{2d-n}; thus \lambda_A(n) is a map A^n\to A^{2d-n}. The same argument with \beta\in B^2 shows \lambda_B(n) maps B^n to B^{2d-n}. For linearity, let t\in\mathbb Q_\ell and x,x'\in A^n. Additivity is clear: \alpha^{d-n}(x+x')=\alpha^{d-n}x+\alpha^{d-n}x' by distributivity in A. For scalars, writing again t for the image of t under the structure map \mathbb Q_\ell\to A, which lands in the centre of A, associativity and centrality give \alpha^{d-n}(tx')=\alpha^{d-n}(t\,x')=\alpha^{d-n}(x' t)=(\alpha^{d-n}x')t=t(\alpha^{d-n}x'). Hence \lambda_A(n) is \mathbb Q_\ell-linear; identically for \lambda_B(n).

Step 2 (the inverse of a graded isomorphism is graded). We record this so that the degree-n component of \varphi^{-1} is defined. Let y\in B^n. Since \varphi is surjective, y=\varphi(x) for some x\in A; write x=\sum_i x_i as a finite sum of homogeneous components x_i\in A^i. As \varphi is a graded homomorphism, \varphi(x_i)\in B^i is homogeneous, and \sum_i\varphi(x_i)=y\in B^n. Because B is a direct sum of its graded pieces, the decomposition of an element into homogeneous components is unique, so \varphi(x_i)=0 for i\neq n and y=\varphi(x_n) with x_n\in A^n. Thus \varphi^{-1}(y)=x_n\in A^n, i.e. \varphi^{-1} preserves degrees. Consequently, for each integer m the degree-m component \varphi_m:A^m\to B^m is a \mathbb Q_\ell-vector-space isomorphism, with inverse (\varphi^{-1})_m:B^m\to A^m.

Step 3 (powers are preserved). We claim that for every m\ge 0 and every x\in A one has \varphi(\alpha^{m}x)=c^{m}\beta^{m}\varphi(x). First, \varphi(\alpha^{0})=\varphi(1_A)=1_B=\varphi(\alpha)^{0}, using that a homomorphism of unital graded \mathbb Q_\ell-algebras preserves the unit. If \varphi(\alpha^{m})=\varphi(\alpha)^{m}, then \varphi(\alpha^{m+1})=\varphi(\alpha^{m}\alpha)=\varphi(\alpha^{m})\varphi(\alpha)=\varphi(\alpha)^{m}\varphi(\alpha)=\varphi(\alpha)^{m+1}, since ring homomorphisms preserve multiplication. By induction \varphi(\alpha^{m})=\varphi(\alpha)^{m} for all m\ge 0. Using again that \varphi preserves multiplication,
\[\varphi(\alpha^{m}x)=\varphi(\alpha^{m})\,\varphi(x)=\varphi(\alpha)^{m}\varphi(x)=(c\beta)^{m}\varphi(x)=c^{m}\beta^{m}\varphi(x),\]
where the last equality holds because c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times} maps into the centre of B, so powers of c\beta are c^{m}\beta^{m}.

Step 4 (the intertwining identity). Fix n with 0\le n\le d and put m=d-n\ge 0. For x\in A^n, applying Step 3 with this m gives
\[(\varphi_{2d-n}\circ\lambda_A(n))(x)=\varphi(\alpha^{m}x)=c^{m}\beta^{m}\varphi(x)=c^{m}\,(\lambda_B(n)\circ\varphi_n)(x).\]
Hence as maps A^n\to B^{2d-n}
\[\varphi_{2d-n}\circ\lambda_A(n)=c^{d-n}\,\lambda_B(n)\circ\varphi_n. \qquad (\ast)\]
Here c^{d-n}\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times} because c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times} and d-n\ge 0 (with c^{0}=1), so multiplication by c^{d-n} is an automorphism of the \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space B^{2d-n}, and the scalar c^{d-n} may be moved across any of the \mathbb Q_\ell-linear maps involved.

Step 5 (conclusion). Compose (\ast) on the right with the isomorphism \varphi_n^{-1}:B^n\to A^n (Step 2). Since the scalar c^{d-n} commutes with everything, we obtain, as maps B^n\to B^{2d-n},
\[\lambda_B(n)=c^{-(d-n)}\circ\varphi_{2d-n}\circ\lambda_A(n)\circ\varphi_n^{-1}.\]
Each factor on the right is a \mathbb Q_\ell-vector-space isomorphism: \varphi_n^{-1} by Step 2, \lambda_A(n) by the hypothesis on A, \varphi_{2d-n} by Step 2, and multiplication by the nonzero scalar c^{-(d-n)}\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}. A composition of isomorphisms is an isomorphism, so \lambda_B(n):B^n\to B^{2d-n}, y\mapsto\beta^{d-n}y, is an isomorphism.

Step 6 (edge cases and generality of the argument). The case d=0 is included: then n=0 and d-n=0, so \lambda_A(0) and \lambda_B(0) are both the identity of A^0 and B^0 respectively (as \alpha^{0}=1_A, \beta^{0}=1_B), and Step 5 reads \lambda_B(0)=\varphi_0\circ\mathrm{id}\circ\varphi_0^{-1}=\mathrm{id}. The argument used only that \varphi is a graded \mathbb Q_\ell-algebra isomorphism, that \alpha and \beta are homogeneous of degree 2, and that c is invertible; in particular no normalisation c=1 was assumed, no commutativity of A or B was used, and no reference to varieties or Frobenius is needed. Since n with 0\le n\le d was arbitrary, the maps B^n\to B^{2d-n}, y\mapsto\beta^{d-n}y, are isomorphisms for all such n, which is the desired conclusion.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, \(\ell\neq p\) prime, \(m\ge1\), \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and \(d\ge2\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(Y\subsetneq X\) be a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\), with closed immersion \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\) and open complement \(j:U=X\setminus Y\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); let \(\xi=\mathrm{cl}(Y)\), let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\) on \(X\) and \(L_Y\) cup product with \(i^*\xi\) on \(Y\). Suppose \(H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for every \(j<d\) and that \(L_Y^{\,d-1-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-2-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le n\le d-1\). Then \(L^{\,d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le n\le d-2\).
proof:
Set Q=q^m. Since Q is again a prime power, every lemma stated for a prime power q may be applied with q replaced by Q. Write H^n(Z)=H^n_et(Z_k,Q_l) for Z in {X,Y,U}, with compact supports for U when indicated. The divisor Y is very ample, hence ample.

1. Low-degree pullback. By lemma_283 (applied over F_Q) there is a long exact sequence
... -> H^n_c(U) -> H^n(X) -> H^n(Y) -> H^{n+1}_c(U) -> ...
whose middle map is i^*:H^n(X)->H^n(Y). Fix n with 0<=n<=d-2. The hypothesis H_c^j(U)=0 for every j<d gives H_c^n(U)=0 and H_c^{n+1}(U)=0. Exactness then implies that i^*:H^n(X)->H^n(Y) is an isomorphism. Record this as (1).

2. Traces and Gysin. By lemma_77 (applied to X and Y over F_Q) the Poincare duality trace maps, composed with the fixed identification of Tate twists with Q_l,
tr_X:H^{2d}(X)->Q_l,   tr_Y:H^{2d-2}(Y)->Q_l,
give perfect pairings
H^n(X) x H^{2d-n}(X) -> Q_l, (x,y) -> tr_X(x cup y),
and
H^n(Y) x H^{2d-2-n}(Y) -> Q_l, (a,b) -> tr_Y(a cup b),
for every n in the relevant range. By lemma_439_gysin_projection_formula_divisor (applied over F_Q) there is a Gysin homomorphism
i_!:H^n(Y)->H^{n+2}(X)
characterised by
tr_X(i_!a cup b)=tr_Y(a cup i^*b)
for all a in H^n(Y) and b in H^{2d-2-n}(X), and satisfying
i_!(i^*x)=x cup xi=Lx
for all x in H^n(X). Also i^*L=L_Y i^*, because i^* is a ring homomorphism and L_Y is cup product with i^*xi.

3. Reduction to a pairing on Y. Fix n with 0<=n<=d-2 and put r=d-n-1. Then r=d-1-n satisfies 0<=r<=d-1. The hypothesis on Y says that
P:=L_Y^r:H^n(Y)->H^{2d-2-n}(Y)
is an isomorphism. Define
T_n=L^{d-n}:H^n(X)->H^{2d-n}(X)
and the bilinear form
B_n(x,z)=tr_X(T_n x cup z),   x,z in H^n(X).
We prove that B_n is nondegenerate. Since T_n=L^r L and L=i_!i^*, we have
T_n x=L^r i_!i^*x.
By graded commutativity of cup product there is a sign epsilon_n in {+1,-1} such that
B_n(x,z)=epsilon_n tr_X(i_!i^*x cup L^r z).
Using the trace characterisation of i_! with a=i^*x and b=L^r z gives
B_n(x,z)=epsilon_n tr_Y(i^*x cup i^*L^r z).
Since i^*L=L_Y i^*, this becomes
B_n(x,z)=epsilon_n tr_Y(i^*x cup L_Y^r i^*z).
Again by graded commutativity on Y there is a sign delta_n in {+1,-1} such that
B_n(x,z)=epsilon_n delta_n tr_Y(L_Y^r i^*z cup i^*x).
Define the pairing on H^n(Y)
K(u,v)=tr_Y(L_Y^r u cup v).
Thus, up to the nonzero scalar epsilon_n delta_n,
B_n(x,z)=K(i^*z,i^*x).

4. The pairing K is perfect. First let u be nonzero. Since P=L_Y^r is injective, Pu is nonzero. By perfectness of the pairing (a,b)->tr_Y(a cup b) between H^n(Y) and H^{2d-2-n}(Y), there exists v in H^n(Y) such that tr_Y(Pu cup v) is nonzero, i.e. K(u,v) is nonzero. Hence K is nondegenerate in the first variable. Now let v be nonzero. By perfectness of the same pairing, there exists w in H^{2d-2-n}(Y) such that tr_Y(w cup v) is nonzero. Since P is surjective, w=Pu for some u in H^n(Y). Then K(u,v)=tr_Y(Pu cup v) is nonzero. Hence K is also nondegenerate in the second variable. Therefore K is a perfect pairing.

5. Nondegeneracy of B_n. Suppose B_n(x,z)=0 for every z. Then K(i^*z,i^*x)=0 for every z. By (1), i^*z ranges over all of H^n(Y), so K(u,i^*x)=0 for every u in H^n(Y). Since K is perfect, i^*x=0, and by (1) x=0. Similarly, suppose B_n(x,z)=0 for every x. Then K(i^*z,u)=0 for every u in H^n(Y). Perfectness of K gives i^*z=0, and by (1) z=0. Thus B_n is nondegenerate in both variables.

6. From nondegeneracy to the desired isomorphism. The perfect pairing on X from lemma_77 identifies H^{2d-n}(X) with the Q_l-linear dual of H^n(X). If T_n x=0, then B_n(x,z)=0 for all z, hence x=0; therefore T_n is injective. If im T_n were a proper subspace of H^{2d-n}(X), choose w in H^{2d-n}(X) not in im T_n. Extend a linear functional on the span of im T_n and w which vanishes on im T_n and is nonzero on w to a linear functional on all of H^{2d-n}(X). By perfectness of the pairing on X, this functional is represented by some z in H^n(X), i.e. tr_X(u cup z)=0 for every u in im T_n and tr_X(w cup z) is nonzero. Then for every x in H^n(X),
B_n(x,z)=tr_X(T_n x cup z)=0,
contradicting nondegeneracy of B_n. Hence im T_n=H^{2d-n}(X), so T_n is surjective. Therefore T_n=L^{d-n}:H^n(X)->H^{2d-n}(X) is an isomorphism.

Since this holds for every integer n with 0<=n<=d-2, the map
L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_l)->H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_l)
is an isomorphism for all such n.

statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(\iota:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\) be an embedding, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, and let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)\). Suppose there exist constants \(C\ge 1\) and \(\rho>0\) such that \(|\iota(\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^{j}))|\le C\,\rho^{j}\) for every integer \(j\ge 1\). Then every eigenvalue \(\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) of \(T\) satisfies \(|\iota(\alpha)|\le\rho\).
proof:
We prove the statement by reducing it to a purely complex-analytic fact about power sums, which we then establish from scratch. The argument is pure linear algebra plus the Ces\`aro-mean (orthogonality) trick for trigonometric polynomials; no external result is needed.

STEP 1. Reduction to complex power sums.
If $V=0$ there are no eigenvalues and the conclusion is vacuous, so assume $n:=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V\ge 1$. Let
$$\chi_T(t)=t^n+c_{n-1}t^{n-1}+\cdots+c_0\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$$\nbe the characteristic polynomial of $T$, and factor it over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$:
$$\chi_T(t)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}(t-\alpha_i),\qquad \alpha_i\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell.$$
Since $\prod_i\alpha_i=(-1)^n c_0=(-1)^n\det(T)\neq 0$ (as $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$), every $\alpha_i$ is non-zero. The multiset $\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\}$ is exactly the multiset of eigenvalues of $T$ on $V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, counted with algebraic multiplicity.

We claim that for every integer $j\ge 1$,
$$\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^{j})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i^{j}\quad\text{in }\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell.\tag{1}$$
Proof of the claim. Extend scalars to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$: put $\overline V:=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ and $\overline T:=T\otimes\mathrm{id}$. Choosing a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-basis of $V$, the matrix of $\overline T^{\,j}$ equals the matrix of $T^j$ with entries viewed in $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$; hence
$$\operatorname{Tr}_{\overline V}(\overline T^{\,j})=\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^{j}).\tag{2}$$
On the other hand $\chi_{\overline T}=\chi_T$ splits as $\prod_i(t-\alpha_i)$, so $\overline T$ is triangularisable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$: there is a basis of $\overline V$ in which $\overline T$ is upper triangular with diagonal entries $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ in some order. In that basis $\overline T^{\,j}$ is again upper triangular (product of upper-triangular matrices), and its diagonal entries are $\alpha_1^{j},\dots,\alpha_n^{j}$ (the diagonal of a product of upper-triangular matrices is the product of the diagonals). The trace of a matrix is the sum of its diagonal entries and is basis-independent, so
$$\operatorname{Tr}_{\overline V}(\overline T^{\,j})=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i^{j},$$\nwhich together with (2) proves (1).

Applying the embedding $\iota:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$, which is a field homomorphism, to (1) gives
$$\iota\!\left(\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^{j})\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\iota(\alpha_i)^{j}\qquad\text{for all }j\ge 1.\tag{3}$$
Put $z_i:=\iota(\alpha_i)\in\mathbb C^{*}$. By hypothesis there are $C\ge 1$ and $\rho>0$ with
$$\Bigl|\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_i^{\,j}\Bigr|=\bigl|\iota(\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^{j}))\bigr|\le C\rho^{j}\qquad\forall j\ge 1.\tag{4}$$
It therefore suffices to prove the following purely complex assertion, which says $\max_i|z_i|\le\rho$; since $\{z_i\}=\{\iota(\alpha):\alpha\text{ an eigenvalue of }T\}$ as multisets, this is exactly the desired conclusion.

CLAIM. Let $z_1,\dots,z_n\in\mathbb C^{*}$, $C\ge 1$, $\rho>0$, and suppose $\bigl|\sum_i z_i^{\,j}\bigr|\le C\rho^{j}$ for every $j\ge 1$. Then $\max_i|z_i|\le\rho$.

PROOF OF THE CLAIM. Suppose for a contradiction that $R:=\max_i|z_i|>\rho$ (in particular $R>0$). Let $\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_s$ be the DISTINCT elements of $\{z_i:|z_i|=R\}$, and let $m_\lambda:=\#\{i:z_i=\gamma_\lambda\}\ge 1$ be the multiplicity of $\gamma_\lambda$ among the $z_i$. Let
$$R':=\max\bigl\{|z_i|:|z_i|<R\bigr\},$$\nwith the convention $R'=0$ if no $z_i$ has modulus $<R$. Then $0\le R'<R$. Decompose the power sums as
$$s_j:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_i^{\,j}=v_j+E_j,\qquad v_j:=\sum_{\lambda=1}^{s}m_\lambda\gamma_\lambda^{\,j},\qquad |E_j|\le n\,(R')^{j},\tag{5}$$\nwhere the bound on $E_j$ counts the at most $n$ terms with modulus $<R$, each of modulus at most $(R')^j$ (if $R'=0$ there are no such terms and $E_j=0=(R')^j$ for $j\ge1$).

Sub-claim. With $w_j:=v_j/R^{j}=\sum_{\lambda=1}^{s}m_\lambda\omega_\lambda^{\,j}$, where $\omega_\lambda:=\gamma_\lambda/R$, one has
$$\limsup_{j\to\infty}|w_j|^{2}\ \ge\ \tfrac12\sum_{\lambda=1}^{s}m_\lambda^{2}\ >\ 0.\tag{6}$$
Note $|\omega_\lambda|=1$ and $\omega_\lambda\ne\omega_\mu$ for $\lambda\ne\mu$ (since the $\gamma_\lambda$ are distinct).

Proof of the sub-claim. For $M\ge 1$ expand the square:
$$\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^{M}|w_j|^{2}=\sum_{\lambda,\mu=1}^{s}m_\lambda m_\mu\,\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^{M}(\omega_\lambda\overline{\omega_\mu})^{j}.$$
For $\lambda=\mu$ we have $\omega_\lambda\overline{\omega_\lambda}=1$, so the inner average equals $1$. For $\lambda\ne\mu$ put $\Omega:=\omega_\lambda\overline{\omega_\mu}$; then $|\Omega|=1$ and $\Omega\ne1$, so the geometric sum satisfies
$$\Bigl|\sum_{j=1}^{M}\Omega^{j}\Bigr|=\frac{|\Omega|\,|1-\Omega^{M}|}{|1-\Omega|}\le\frac{2}{|1-\Omega|},$$\nhence $\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^{M}\Omega^{j}\to0$ as $M\to\infty$. Therefore
$$\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^{M}|w_j|^{2}\xrightarrow[M\to\infty]{}\sum_{\lambda=1}^{s}m_\lambda^{2}=:S,$$\nand $S\ge 1$ because $s\ge1$ and each $m_\lambda\ge1$. Also $|w_j|\le\sum_\lambda m_\lambda$, so the sequence $(|w_j|^2)$ is bounded, say by $B$. If $|w_j|^2<S/2$ held for all $j\ge J$, then for $M>J$,
$$\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^{M}|w_j|^{2}\le\frac{J}{M}B+\frac{S}{2}\Bigl(1-\frac JM\xrightarrow[M\to\infty]{}\frac S2,$$\ncontradicting convergence to $S$. Hence $\{j:|w_j|^2\ge S/2\}$ is infinite, proving (6).

Conclusion of the claim. By (6) there are arbitrarily large $j$ with $|v_j|=|w_j|R^{j}\ge c_0R^{j}$, where $c_0:=\sqrt{S/2}>0$. Since $0\le R'/R<1$, we have $n(R')^{j}\le \frac{c_0}{2}R^{j}$ for all $j\ge J_0$. Intersecting the two (infinite/cofinite) sets of indices, we obtain arbitrarily large $j$ such that, by (5),
$$|s_j|\ge |v_j|-|E_j|\ge c_0R^{j}-\frac{c_0}{2}R^{j}=\frac{c_0}{2}R^{j}=:c\,R^{j},\qquad c>0.$$
Combining with the hypothesis (4) gives $cR^{j}\le C\rho^{j}$, i.e. $(R/\rho)^{j}\le C/c$, for arbitrarily large $j$. But $R>\rho$ means $R/\rho>1$, so $(R/\rho)^{j}\to\infty$, a contradiction. Hence $R\le\rho$. This proves the claim. $\diamondsuit$

STEP 2. End of the proof.
Applying the claim to $z_i=\iota(\alpha_i)$ yields $\max_i|\iota(\alpha_i)|\le\rho$. Finally, let $\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ be any eigenvalue of $T$ (i.e. of $T$ on $V\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$). Then $\alpha$ is a root of $\chi_T$, hence $\alpha=\alpha_i$ for some $i$, and therefore $|\iota(\alpha)|=|\iota(\alpha_i)|\le\rho$. This is exactly the required conclusion. $\blacksquare$

(Remark on the role of the hypotheses: $C\ge1$ is used only to keep the constants harmless, and invertibility of $T$ is used only to ensure $\alpha_i\ne0$; the latter is in fact not needed for the claim, since the argument only requires $R>\rho>0$ to normalise by $R^j$.)

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), put \(Q=q^m\) and \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(C\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over \(\mathbb F_{Q}\), and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_{C_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{Q}\), be the \(Q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then the multiset of eigenvalues of \(F\) on \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), counted with algebraic multiplicity, is invariant under \(\alpha\mapsto Q/\alpha\).
proof:
We prove the statement by an argument carried out entirely in cohomology: Poincar\'e duality for the curve makes the cup product a perfect pairing on $H^1$ on which the $Q$-power Frobenius is a similitude of factor $Q$, and then the purely linear-algebraic part (3) of lemma_69 turns the relation $F^{\dagger}=QF^{-1}$ into the claimed symmetry of the eigenvalue multiset. No semisimplicity and no positivity/Hasse--Weil input is used.

**Step 1: Notation and the finite-dimensionality/invertibility of $F$.**
Put $Q=q^m=p^{am}$; since $a\ge1$ and $m\ge1$, $Q$ is a prime power and $\mathbb F_Q=\mathbb F_{q^m}$. Also $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q=\overline{\mathbb F}_{p^a}=\overline{\mathbb F}_{p^{am}}=\overline{\mathbb F}_Q$. Write
\[
 V:=H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).
\]
Since $C$ is proper over $\mathbb F_Q$, applying lemma_45_finite_frob to the proper $\mathbb F_Q$-scheme $C$ (the lemma is stated over a finite field, so we use it with the field $\mathbb F_Q$ in place of its $\mathbb F_q$) and the constant sheaf $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism shows that $V=H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$.

Applying lemma_6a to the $\mathbb F_Q$-scheme $C$ (again with $\mathbb F_Q$ in place of its $\mathbb F_q$, so that $\sigma(c)=c^Q$) gives that $F_{\mathrm{ar}}=(\mathrm{id}_{C_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$; this is exactly the operator $F$ of the statement. Hence $F\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$; in particular every eigenvalue of $F$ is nonzero (its eigenvalues $\alpha_i$ satisfy $\prod_i\alpha_i=\pm\det(F)\ne0$).

**Step 2: The case $V=0$.**
If $V=0$ (the genus-$0$ case), then $V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell=0$, the multiset of eigenvalues of $F$ is empty, and the assertion that this multiset is invariant under $\alpha\mapsto Q/\alpha$ is vacuously true. Henceforth assume $V\ne0$, so that lemma_69 is applicable.

**Step 3: The Frobenius-equivariant perfect pairing on $H^1$.**
Apply lemma_77 with $Y=C$ (smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension $d=1$ over $\mathbb F_{q^m}=\mathbb F_Q$), with $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$ and with $F$ the $q^m$-power arithmetic Frobenius, which is precisely the operator of the statement. Its part (a) provides the trace isomorphism
\[
 \operatorname{tr}:H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)
\]
(normalised by $\operatorname{tr}(\mathrm{cl}(x))=[k(x):\mathbb F_{q^m}]$ on closed points), and its part (b), applied to $n=1$ and $2d-n=1$, says that
\[
 \langle v,w\rangle:=\operatorname{tr}(v\cup w)\;\in\;\mathbb Q_\ell(-1),\qquad v,w\in V,
\]\nis a PERFECT $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinear pairing $V\times V\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)$, and that
\[
 \langle Fv,Fw\rangle=q^{m\cdot 1}\langle v,w\rangle=Q\,\langle v,w\rangle\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V,
\]\nwhere $q^{md}=q^{m}=Q$ is viewed as a positive rational number, hence as an element of $\mathbb Q_\ell^{*}$ (it is nonzero because $\ell\ne p$).

**Step 4: Trivialising the target so as to get a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-valued pairing.**
Fix any $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $\varphi:\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$ (existence: $\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)$ is a one-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space; no Frobenius-equivariance of $\varphi$ is required or claimed). Define
\[
 \beta:V\times V\longrightarrow\mathbb Q_\ell,\qquad \beta(v,w):=\varphi\bigl(\langle v,w\rangle\bigr).
\]
Because $\langle\ ,\ \rangle$ is perfect and $\varphi$ is an isomorphism, $\beta$ is a perfect $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinear pairing: for each nonzero $v\in V$ the map $w\mapsto\langle v,w\rangle$ is a nonzero element of $V^{\vee}$, and composing with the isomorphism $\varphi$ keeps it nonzero. Moreover, applying the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map $\varphi$ to the identity of Step 3 gives
\[
 \beta(Fv,Fw)=Q\,\beta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V. \tag{$*$}
\]

**Step 5: The adjoint relation $F^{\dagger}=QF^{-1}$.**
We are now in the situation of lemma_69 with $k=\mathbb Q_\ell$, $T=F\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, $c=Q\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{*}$, and the perfect pairing $\beta$. By lemma_69(0) the adjoint $a\mapsto a^{\dagger}$, defined by $\beta(av,w)=\beta(v,a^{\dagger}w)$ for all $v,w$, exists and is unique. We verify the hypothesis $F^{\dagger}=QF^{-1}$ of lemma_69 directly: for all $v,w\in V$, using $(*)$ in the second and third steps and the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinearity of $\beta$ throughout,
\[
 \beta(Fv,w)=\beta\bigl(Fv,\,F(F^{-1}w)\bigr)=Q\,\beta\bigl(v,F^{-1}w\bigr)=\beta\bigl(v,\,QF^{-1}w\bigr).
\]
Since $Fv$ and $w$ range over all of $V$ as $v,w$ do, the defining property of the adjoint together with its uniqueness (lemma_69(0)) yields
\[
 F^{\dagger}=Q\,F^{-1}.
\]

**Step 6: Conclusion via lemma_69(3).**
Apply lemma_69 to $V$, $T=F$ and $c=Q$: its part (3) states that if $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_N\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell^{\,*}$ are the eigenvalues of $T$ on $V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ counted with algebraic multiplicity, then the multisets $\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_N\}$ and $\{c/\alpha_1,\dots,c/\alpha_N\}$ coincide with multiplicities (the proof there needs no semisimplicity: $F^{\dagger}$ is similar to the transpose $F^{t}$, so $\chi_{F^{\dagger}}=\chi_F$, while by part (2) applied to the Laurent polynomial $P(t)=Qt^{-1}$ the eigenvalues of $F^{\dagger}=QF^{-1}$ are $Q/\alpha_1,\dots,Q/\alpha_N$; unique factorisation in $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]$ concludes). With $c=Q$ this says exactly that the multiset of eigenvalues of $F$ on $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, counted with algebraic multiplicity, is invariant under $\alpha\mapsto Q/\alpha$.

Together with Step 2 this covers both possibilities for $V$, and the lemma is proved. \qed

(Remarks on what was and was not used: the pairing $\beta$ is in fact alternating, by the graded-commutativity of the cup product in degree $1$, but lemma_69(3) needs no symmetry hypothesis, so nothing depends on this. No positivity statement, Hasse--Weil bound, or Rosati-trace estimate was invoked, and no eigenvalue transfer between $V_\ell(\operatorname{Jac}C)$ and $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ was performed; the whole argument lives on cohomology, with the scalar $Q$ coming from the Frobenius action on $\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)$ as recorded in lemma_77(b).)

statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, \(\iota:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\) an embedding, \(V\neq0\) a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, \(c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}\) with \(\iota(c)>0\), and \(\langle\,,\,\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) a perfect bilinear pairing. Let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)\) satisfy \(\langle Tv,Tw\rangle=c\langle v,w\rangle\) for all \(v,w\in V\). Then the multiset of real numbers \(\{|\iota(\alpha)|\}\), as \(\alpha\) runs over the eigenvalues of \(T\) in \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) with algebraic multiplicity, is invariant under \(t\mapsto\iota(c)/t\). Consequently, if there is a real \(\rho>0\) with \(|\iota(\alpha)|\le\rho\) for every eigenvalue \(\alpha\), then \(|\iota(\alpha)|\ge\iota(c)/\rho\) for every eigenvalue; in particular, taking \(\rho=\iota(c)^{1/2}\), the single estimate \(|\iota(\alpha)|\le\iota(c)^{1/2}\) for all \(\alpha\) forces \(|\iota(\alpha)|=\iota(c)^{1/2}\) for all \(\alpha\).
proof:
Write $k=\mathbb Q_\ell$, $\bar k=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, and $N=\dim_k V\ge 1$ (the latter since $V\neq 0$). Let $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_N\in\bar k$ be the eigenvalues of $T$ counted with algebraic multiplicity; these are the roots of the characteristic polynomial $\chi_T\in k[t]$, which has degree $N\ge1$, so the list is non-empty and each $\alpha_i$ lies in $\bar k$, where $\iota$ is defined.

**Step 1: the adjoint of $T$.** By part (0) of eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_69, the perfectness of $\langle\,,\,\rangle$ guarantees that for every $a\in\operatorname{End}_k(V)$ there is a *unique* adjoint $a^\dagger\in\operatorname{End}_k(V)$ with
