The hypotheses already supply the commuting multiplicative factorisation F = F_sF_u = F_uF_s with F_s semisimple and F_u unipotent (such a pair exists by the Jordan--Chevalley theorem for \operatorname{GL} over the characteristic-zero field \mathbb Q_\ell; we take it as given and make no use of the additive Jordan--Chevalley decomposition).

Preliminaries: consequences of the given factorisation.
(a) Put T := F_u - \operatorname{id}. "F_u is unipotent" means precisely that T is nilpotent. By the assumption F_u \neq \operatorname{id} we have T \neq 0. The set \{m \ge 1 : T^m = 0\} is non-empty (T is nilpotent) and does not contain 1 (T \neq 0); let M \ge 2 be its minimum, so that T^M = 0 and T^{M-1} \neq 0.
(b) F_u = \operatorname{id} + T is invertible, with inverse the finite geometric series in T:
    G := \sum_{k=0}^{M-1} (-1)^k T^k.
Indeed (\operatorname{id}+T)G = \sum_{k=0}^{M-1}(-1)^kT^k + \sum_{k=1}^{M}(-1)^{k-1}T^k = \operatorname{id} + (-1)^{M-1}T^M = \operatorname{id}, and likewise G(\operatorname{id}+T)=\operatorname{id}, using T^M=0. Thus G = F_u^{-1} is a polynomial in T, hence a polynomial in F_u; consequently F_u^{-1} commutes with T, with F_u, and with every operator that commutes with F_u.
(c) F_s is invertible, because F_s = F F_u^{-1} is a product of two invertible operators (F \in \operatorname{GL}_K(V) and F_u^{-1} from (b)). From F_sF_u = F_uF_s, multiplying on the left by F_s^{-1} gives F_u = F_s^{-1}F_uF_s, and multiplying that on the right by F_s^{-1} gives F_uF_s^{-1} = F_s^{-1}F_u; so F_s^{-1} commutes with F_u. Combining with (b), the five operators F, F_s, F_s^{-1}, F_u, F_u^{-1} pairwise commute (F = F_sF_u commutes with F_s by the hypothesis F_sF_u=F_uF_s and with F_u trivially, and F^{-1} = F_u^{-1}F_s^{-1} commutes with all of them).

Step 1: N is a well-defined polynomial in T.
For j \ge M we have T^j = T^{M}T^{j-M} = 0, so every term of the series \sum_{j\ge1}(-1)^{j+1}T^j/j with j \ge M vanishes. Hence the series is in fact the finite sum
    N = \sum_{j=1}^{M-1} (-1)^{j+1} T^j / j \in K[T] \subseteq \operatorname{End}_K(V),
a polynomial in T with zero constant term.

Step 2: N is nilpotent.
N lies in the ideal (T) of the commutative K-algebra K[T]. Expanding N^M as a K-linear combination of products T^{j_1}T^{j_2}\cdots T^{j_M} with each j_i \in \{1,\dots,M-1\}, each such product equals T^{j_1+\cdots+j_M} with j_1+\cdots+j_M \ge M, hence is 0 because T^M = 0. Therefore N^M = 0, i.e. N is nilpotent.

Step 3: N \neq 0.
Factor T out of the polynomial in Step 1:
    N = T\Big(\operatorname{id} + \sum_{j=2}^{M-1}(-1)^{j+1}T^{j-1}/j\Big) = T(\operatorname{id} + TR), \qquad R := \sum_{j=2}^{M-1}(-1)^{j+1}T^{j-2}/j,
where R := 0 if M = 2 (the empty sum). Set U := \operatorname{id} + TR. Since T^M = 0 we have (TR)^M = T^MR^M = 0, so TR is nilpotent and U is invertible, with inverse \sum_{k=0}^{M-1}(-1)^k(TR)^k (the same computation as in (b)). If N were 0, then multiplying N = TU on the right by U^{-1} would give T = 0, contradicting (a). Hence N \neq 0.

Step 4: F and F_s commute with T by conjugation.
Using (c),
    F F_u F^{-1} = (F_sF_u)F_u(F_u^{-1}F_s^{-1}) = F_sF_uF_s^{-1} = F_u,
where the last equality holds because F_s commutes with F_u. Hence
    FTF^{-1} = F(F_u-\operatorname{id})F^{-1} = F_u - \operatorname{id} = T.
Similarly, F_sF_uF_s^{-1} = F_u by commutativity, so
    F_sTF_s^{-1} = F_sF_uF_s^{-1} - \operatorname{id} = F_u - \operatorname{id} = T.

Step 5: FNF^{-1} = N.
Conjugation by the invertible operator F, namely \operatorname{Ad}_F : A \mapsto FAF^{-1}, is a K-algebra automorphism of \operatorname{End}_K(V): it is K-linear, multiplicative, and sends \operatorname{id} to \operatorname{id}. By Step 4 it fixes \operatorname{id} and T, hence it fixes every element of the subalgebra K[T], in particular the polynomial N of Step 1. Thus FNF^{-1} = N. (Equivalently, this is the case q = 1 of eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_506 applied with K = \mathbb Q_\ell and T := F_u, whose hypothesis FTF^{-1}=T^1 is exactly the identity of Step 4; the argument above is self-contained and no external input is needed.)

Step 6: F_sN = NF_s.
By Step 4, F_sTF_s^{-1} = T, i.e. F_sT = TF_s. Hence F_sT^j = T^jF_s for every j \ge 0, and by K-linearity F_s commutes with every polynomial in T. Since N \in K[T] by Step 1, F_sN = NF_s.

Steps 1--6 establish the first assertion: if F_u \neq \operatorname{id}_V then N = \log F_u is a nonzero nilpotent element of \operatorname{End}_K(V) with FNF^{-1} = N and F_sN = NF_s.

Step 7: the consequence.
Assume that the only nilpotent A \in \operatorname{End}_K(V) satisfying FAF^{-1} = A is A = 0. We show F is semisimple. If F_u = \operatorname{id}_V, then F = F_sF_u = F_s is semisimple, and we are done. If instead F_u \neq \operatorname{id}_V, then Steps 1, 2 and 5 produce a nonzero nilpotent N \in \operatorname{End}_K(V) with FNF^{-1} = N, contradicting the assumption. Hence F_u = \operatorname{id}_V and F = F_s is semisimple on V.

This completes the proof. (The hypothesis that V is nonzero is not needed for the argument: for V = 0 one has F_u = \operatorname{id}, so the antecedent F_u \neq \operatorname{id} is false and the statement is vacuous, while the consequence in Step 7 is likewise immediate.)

statement:
Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime,

let \(m\ge1\) be an integer and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(f:Y\to X\) be a proper surjective generically finite morphism of degree \(N\ge1\) between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(\mathcal A\) be an \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-rational ample line bundle on \(X\), let \(\xi=\mathrm{cl}(\mathcal A)\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), and let \(L_X\) be cup product with \(\xi\). Put \(\mathcal A_Y=f^*\mathcal A\), \(\xi_Y=\mathrm{cl}(\mathcal A_Y)\), and let \(L_Y\) be cup product with \(\xi_Y\). If \(L_Y^{\,d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le n\le d\), then \(L_X^{\,d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le n\le d\).
proof:
Proof. Set Q=q^m. Then Q=p^{am} is a prime power and k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q=\overline{\mathbb F}_Q. For Z=X,Y write H^n(Z)=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). The fixed nonzero element of \mathbb Q_\ell(1) is used to identify Tate twists with \mathbb Q_\ell; the same identification is used for X and Y. In particular the Poincare duality traces are composed with the resulting identifications \mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell. If d=0, then 0\le n\le d forces n=0 and L_X^{0}=\operatorname{id}, so the assertion is immediate. Assume d\ge1.

First we record the naturality of the cycle class of a line bundle. For a smooth projective variety Z, the class cl(\mathcal L) of a line bundle \mathcal L is the first Chern class obtained as the compatible inverse limit of the connecting homomorphisms \delta_n:\operatorname{Pic}(Z)\to H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z,\mu_{\ell^n}) coming from the Kummer sequences 0\to\mu_{\ell^n}\to\mathbb G_m\xrightarrow{\ell^n}\mathbb G_m\to0. Pullback of sheaves is exact and commutes with the connecting homomorphisms in the long exact cohomology sequence; hence \delta_n(f^*\mathcal L)=f^*\delta_n(\mathcal L) for every n. The transition maps in the inverse system are also compatible with pullback, so passing to the inverse limit and applying the fixed identification \mathbb Q_\ell(1)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell gives cl(f^*\mathcal L)=f^*cl(\mathcal L). Therefore f^*\xi=f^*cl(\mathcal A)=cl(f^*\mathcal A)=\xi_Y. Since pullback is a ring homomorphism, for every integer s\ge0 and every x\in H^n(X),
 f^*(\xi^{s}\cup x)=(f^*\xi)^{s}\cup f^*x=\xi_Y^{s}\cup f^*x,
so f^*L_X^s=L_Y^sf^*.

Next construct the Gysin pushforward. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77, applied with the prime power Q, the Poincare duality trace maps tr_X:H^{2d}(X)\to\mathbb Q_\ell and tr_Y:H^{2d}(Y)\to\mathbb Q_\ell are normalized by tr_Z(cl(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_Q] for closed points z, and for every r the pairing H^r(Z)\times H^{2d-r}(Z)\to\mathbb Q_\ell, (u,v)\mapsto tr_Z(u\cup v), is perfect. The morphism f:Y\to X is surjective, hence dominant, and is generically finite of degree N. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_194, applied to f:Y\to X over \mathbb F_Q, for each r there is a unique \mathbb Q_\ell-linear map f_*:H^r(Y)\to H^r(X) such that
 tr_X(f_*a\cup b)=tr_Y(a\cup f^*b)
for all a\in H^r(Y) and b\in H^{2d-r}(X). By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_196, applied to the same morphism and this map f_*, one has
 f_*f^*=N\operatorname{id}
on every H^r(X). Since N is a nonzero integer, N is a unit of \mathbb Q_\ell.

We prove the projection formula for f_* and the Lefschetz operator. Let 0\le r\le 2d-2, a\in H^r(Y), and b\in H^{2d-r-2}(X). Using the defining property of f_*, graded commutativity of the cup product (the class moved has degree 2, hence no sign), and the fact that f^* is a ring homomorphism, we compute
 tr_X(f_*(\xi_Y\cup a)\cup b)
 =tr_Y((\xi_Y\cup a)\cup f^*b)
 =tr_Y(a\cup\xi_Y\cup f^*b)
 =tr_Y(a\cup f^*(\xi\cup b))
 =tr_X(f_*a\cup(\xi\cup b))
 =tr_X((\xi\cup f_*a)\cup b).
The perfectness of the pairing on H^{r+2}(X)\times H^{2d-r-2}(X) implies
 f_*(\xi_Y\cup a)=\xi\cup f_*a.
Equivalently, f_*L_Y=L_Xf_* on H^r(Y) for every 0\le r\le 2d-2.

We now prove by induction on s that for every integer s\ge0 and every n with 0\le n\le d-s, one has f_*L_Y^s=L_X^sf_* on H^n. For s=0 this is the identity. Assume the statement for some s<d, and let n\le d-s-1 and a\in H^n. The class L_Y^s a lies in H^{n+2s}(Y). Since n\le d-s-1, we have n+2s\le d+s-1\le 2d-2, so the projection formula applies to L_Y^s a. Therefore
 f_*L_Y^{s+1}a
 =f_*(\xi_Y\cup L_Y^s a)
 =\xi\cup f_*L_Y^s a
 =\xi\cup L_X^sf_*a
 =L_X^{s+1}f_*a,
where the induction hypothesis was used in the third equality. This proves the induction step.

Now fix n with 0\le n\le d and put s=d-n. We show that L_X^s:H^n(X)\to H^{2d-n}(X) is an isomorphism.

Injectivity. Let x\in H^n(X) with L_X^s x=0. Applying f^* and using f^*L_X^s=L_Y^sf^* gives L_Y^sf^*x=0. The hypothesis says L_Y^s is an isomorphism, hence injective, so f^*x=0. Then N x=f_*f^*x=0. Since N is invertible in \mathbb Q_\ell, x=0.

Surjectivity. Let y\in H^{2d-n}(X). Since L_Y^s is surjective, there exists a\in H^n(Y) with L_Y^s a=f^*y. Applying f_* and using f_*L_Y^s=L_X^sf_* gives
 N y=f_*f^*y=f_*L_Y^s a=L_X^s f_*a.
Set x=N^{-1}f_*a\in H^n(X). Then L_X^s x=y. Thus L_X^s is surjective.

Since L_X^{d-n} is both injective and surjective for every 0\le n\le d, it is an isomorphism for every such n. This is exactly the required conclusion.

statement: Let q = p^a be a prime power and let l != p be prime. Suppose that for every integer d >= 1, every m >= 1, and every smooth projective geometrically connected variety X of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id_{X_k} x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^d_et(X_k,Q_l). Then for every integer m >= 1, every smooth projective geometrically connected variety X of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, and every integer n >= 0, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k,Q_l).
proof:
We prove by induction on d >= 0 the statement P(d): for every m >= 1, every smooth projective geometrically connected variety X of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, and every n >= 0, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F_X = (id_{X_k} x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k,Q_l), where k = overline(F_q). The zero vector space is regarded as semisimple for the zero operator.

Base case d = 0. Let X be smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension 0 over F_{q^m}. A smooth morphism of relative dimension 0 is unramified and flat, hence quasi-finite; projectivity gives properness, and a proper quasi-finite morphism is finite. Thus X is finite etale over F_{q^m}. Since X is connected and reduced, X = Spec L for a finite separable field extension L/F_{q^m}. Geometric connectedness means L tensor_{F_{q^m}} k is connected. If [L:F_{q^m}] = r > 1, then, because k is algebraically closed and L/F_{q^m} is finite separable, L tensor k is a product of r copies of k, hence disconnected. Therefore r = 1 and X = Spec F_{q^m}. Then X_k = Spec k.

Since k is separably closed, its absolute Galois group is trivial. Hence for each r >= 1, H^0_et(Spec k,Z/l^r)=Z/l^r and H^n_et(Spec k,Z/l^r)=0 for n > 0. Taking inverse limits over r and tensoring with Q_l, in the usual definition of l-adic cohomology with Q_l coefficients, gives H^0_et(Spec k,Q_l)=Q_l and H^n_et(Spec k,Q_l)=0 for n > 0. The morphism F_X is Spec sigma on Spec k. It pulls back the constant Q_l sheaf to itself and induces the identity on global sections Q_l. Thus F_X is the identity on H^0 and the zero operator on the zero spaces H^n for n > 0, hence semisimple. This proves P(0).

Base case d = 1. Let X be smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension 1 over F_{q^m}. For n = 0 and n = 2, apply Lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_265 with the prime power q^m in place of q. It says that the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius acts as the identity on H^0_et(X_k,Q_l) and as multiplication by (q^m)^1 on H^2_et(X_k,Q_l); scalar operators are semisimple. For n = 1, the desired semisimplicity is exactly the hypothesis of the target lemma, applied to dimension d = 1. For n > 2, X_k is a projective scheme over the algebraically closed field k of pure dimension 1, so by Lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing, H^n_et(X_k,Q_l)=0; the zero operator is semisimple. Thus P(1) holds.

Inductive step. Assume P(d-1) for some integer d >= 2. Fix m >= 1 and a smooth projective geometrically connected variety X of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let F_X denote the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. For every n >= 0 with n != d, apply Lemma eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/d0ddec. Its hypothesis is precisely P(d-1): for every m' >= 1 and every smooth projective geometrically connected Y of pure dimension d-1 over F_{q^{m'}}, the q^{m'}-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on all H^n_et(Y_k,Q_l). The conclusion of that lemma gives semisimplicity of F_X on H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) for all n != d. For n = d, the semisimplicity of F_X on H^d_et(X_k,Q_l) is exactly the assumed middle-degree semisimplicity hypothesis of the target lemma, applied to this d, m, and X. Hence F_X is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) for every n >= 0, proving P(d).

By induction P(d) holds for all d >= 0, which is precisely the desired conclusion.

statement: Let q = p^a be a prime power, let l != p be prime, let m >= 1, and let k be an algebraic closure of F_q. Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d >= 2 over F_{q^m}, and let Y subset X be a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor defined over F_{q^m}, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d-1, with closed immersion i:Y->X. Then for every integer n with 0 <= n <= d-1, the pullback i^*:H^n_et(X_k,Q_l)->H^n_et(Y_k,Q_l) is an isomorphism if n < d-1 and is injective if n = d-1.
proof:
Write K := \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Since \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) contains \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), it is a field extension of \(K\); it is algebraic over \(K\) (being algebraic over \(\mathbb F_q\)) and algebraically closed, and \(\operatorname{char} k=p\neq\ell\). All base changes below are taken along the given embedding \(K\hookrightarrow k\): \(X_k:=X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}K}\operatorname{Spec}k\), \(Y_k:=Y\times_{\operatorname{Spec}K}\operatorname{Spec}k\). The base change of the closed immersion \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\) along \(\operatorname{pr}:X_k\to X\) is \(Y\times_K k=Y_k\hookrightarrow X\times_K k=X_k\); this is exactly the pullback map \(i^*\) appearing in the statement, so it suffices to prove the geometric Lefschetz statement for \(Y_k\subset X_k\).

We first record two elementary facts that will be used for both \(X_k\) and \(Y_k\).

CLAIM 1 (dimension is preserved by algebraic field extension). Let \(W\) be a noetherian scheme of finite type over \(K\) and \(W_k:=W\times_K k\). Then \(\dim W_k=\dim W\).
Proof. The morphism \(\operatorname{pr}:W_k\to W\) is the base change of \(\operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}K\). The ring map \(K\to k\) is integral because \(k\) is algebraic over \(K\); integrality is preserved under base change, so \(\operatorname{pr}\) is integral. The map \(\operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}K\) is surjective (both are one-point spaces), and surjectivity is preserved under base change, so \(\operatorname{pr}\) is surjective.
We show that an integral surjective morphism \(f:Z\to W\) satisfies \(\dim Z=\dim W\), comparing chains of irreducible closed subsets (equivalently, chains of points under specialization).
(\(\ge\)) Let \(\eta_0,\dots,\eta_n\) be points of \(W\) with \(\eta_i\in\overline{\{\eta_{i+1}\}\}\) strictly for each \(i\) (a chain of length \(n\)). Choose a point \(\eta_n'\in Z\) with \(f(\eta_n')=\eta_n\) (lying over). Given \(\eta_{i+1}'\) over \(\eta_{i+1}\), going-up for the integral extension of local rings (equivalently, going-up for integral ring extensions: for \(A\subset B\) integral, \(\mathfrak q_{i+1}\subset B\) and \(\mathfrak p_i\subseteq\mathfrak q_{i+1}\cap A\) there is \(\mathfrak q_i\subseteq\mathfrak q_{i+1}\) with \(\mathfrak q_i\cap A=\mathfrak p_i\)) produces \(\eta_i'\in\overline{\{\eta_{i+1}'\}\}\) with \(f(\eta_i')=\eta_i\). The inclusions are strict, since equality of two consecutive \(\eta_i'\) would force equality of their images. Thus chains of any length in \(W\) lift, so \(\dim Z\ge\dim W\).
(\(\le\)) Let \(\zeta_0\subsetneq\dots\subsetneq\zeta_n\) be a chain of points of \(Z\) under specialization. Their images \(f(\zeta_i)\) satisfy \(f(\zeta_i)\in\overline{\{f(\zeta_{i+1})\}\}\). If \(f(\zeta_i)=f(\zeta_{i+1})\) for some \(i\), work in an affine open \(\operatorname{Spec}A\subset W\) containing the common image and write \(f^{-1}(\operatorname{Spec}A)=\operatorname{Spec}B\) with \(B\) integral over \(A\); then \(\zeta_i,\zeta_{i+1}\) correspond to primes \(\mathfrak q_i\subseteq\mathfrak q_{i+1}\) of \(B\) with the same contraction to \(A\), and incomparability for integral extensions (Atiyah--Macdonald, Cor.~5.9: primes of an integral extension lying over a given prime are incomparable) forces \(\mathfrak q_i=\mathfrak q_{i+1}\), contradiction. Hence the images form a chain of the same length, and \(\dim Z\le\dim W\). \(\square\)

CLAIM 2 (a noetherian scheme with domain local rings has open irreducible components; in particular a connected one is integral). Let \(Z\) be a noetherian scheme such that \(\mathcal O_{Z,z}\) is a domain for every \(z\in Z\). Then every irreducible component of \(Z\) is open; if moreover \(Z\) is connected, then \(Z\) is integral.
Proof. Let \(Z_0\) be an irreducible component and \(z\in Z_0\). Choose an affine open neighbourhood \(U=\operatorname{Spec}A\) of \(z\). Then \(A\) is noetherian and \(A_{\mathfrak p}\cong\mathcal O_{Z,\mathfrak p}\) is a domain for every prime \(\mathfrak p\). In particular \(A\) is reduced (a ring whose localisations at all primes are domains is reduced). Let \(\operatorname{Min}(A)=\{\mathfrak q_1,\dots,\mathfrak q_t\}\); this set is finite because \(A\) is noetherian. For any prime \(\mathfrak p\), the minimal primes of \(A_{\mathfrak p}\) correspond bijectively to the minimal primes of \(A\) contained in \(\mathfrak p\); since \(A_{\mathfrak p}\) is a domain it has exactly one minimal prime, so \(\mathfrak p\) contains exactly one \(\mathfrak q_j\). Consequently \(\mathfrak q_j+\mathfrak q_{j'}=A\) for \(j\neq j'\) (otherwise a maximal ideal would contain both). Since \(\bigcap_j\mathfrak q_j=\operatorname{Nil}(A)=0\), the Chinese remainder theorem gives \(A\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\prod_{j=1}^{t}A/\mathfrak q_j\), hence \(U=\coprod_j U_j\) with \(U_j:=V(\mathfrak q_j)=\operatorname{Spec}(A/\mathfrak q_j)\) an integral subset which is both open and closed in \(U\).
Let \(U_j\) be the piece containing \(z\). The closed irreducible subset \(Z_0\cap U\subseteq U\) contains \(z\), and being irreducible it is contained in a single piece of the disjoint union, so \(Z_0\cap U\subseteq U_j\). On the other hand \(U_j\) is irreducible, so its closure \(\overline{U_j}\) in \(Z\) is irreducible and closed and contains \(z\); by maximality of the component through \(z\), \(\overline{U_j}\subseteq Z_0\). Therefore \(U_j\subseteq\overline{U_j}\cap U\subseteq Z_0\cap U\subseteq U_j\), i.e.\(U_j=Z_0\cap U\). Thus \(Z_0\) contains the open set \(U_j\ni z\), so \(Z_0\) is a neighbourhood of \(z\); as \(z\) was arbitrary, \(Z_0\) is open.
Finally, a noetherian topological space has only finitely many irreducible components \(Z_1,\dots,Z_s\) (otherwise one builds an infinite strictly decreasing chain of closed subsets by successively removing components). Each \(Z_i\) is closed by definition and open by the above, so they form a partition of \(Z\) into disjoint non-empty clopen subsets. If \(Z\) is connected then \(s=1\), i.e.\(Z\) is irreducible; combined with reducedness (all local rings are domains) this says \(Z\) is integral. \(\square\)

STEP 1. \(X_k\) is an integral projective variety over \(k\) of pure dimension \(d\).
(a) \(X\to\operatorname{Spec}K\) is smooth, and smoothness is stable under arbitrary base change, so \(X_k\) is smooth over \(k\). In particular \(X_k\) is of finite type over \(k\), hence noetherian, and every local ring of \(X_k\) is regular.
(b) A regular local ring \((R,\mathfrak m)\) of dimension \(r\) has \(\operatorname{gr}_{\mathfrak m}R\cong(R/\mathfrak m)[T_1,\dots,T_r]\) (regular system of parameters), which is a domain; the initial-form map is then multiplicative on non-zero elements, so \(ab=0\) with \(a,b\neq0\) is impossible. Hence regular local rings are domains, and every local ring of \(X_k\) is a domain.
(c) \(X_k\) is connected: \(X\) is geometrically connected over \(K\) and \(k/K\) is a field extension.
(d) By Claim 2 applied to \(Z=X_k\), \(X_k\) is integral.
(e) \(\dim X_k=\dim X=d\) by Claim 1 (note \(\dim X=d\) since \(X\) has pure dimension \(d\)). Since \(X_k\) is integral its only irreducible component is \(X_k\) itself, which has dimension \(d\); hence \(X_k\) is of pure dimension \(d\ge2\).
(f) \(X_k\) is projective over \(k\) (base change of the projective morphism \(X\to\operatorname{Spec}K\)), hence separated and of finite type; being integral it is reduced, so it is a variety over \(k\).
(g) \(X_k\) is geometrically connected over \(k\): for any field extension \(k\subset K'\), \(X_k\times_k K'=X\times_K K'\), which is connected because \(X\) is geometrically connected over \(K\).

STEP 2. \(Y_k\) is a non-empty effective ample Cartier divisor in \(X_k\), smooth of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(k\), with \(Y_k\subsetneq X_k\).
(a) \(Y_k\to X_k\) is a closed immersion (base change of the closed immersion \(i\)), and \(Y_k=Y\times_K k\) as \(k\)-schemes.
(b) Effective Cartier divisor. Let \(\mathcal I\subset\mathcal O_X\) be the invertible ideal of \(Y\); locally on an affine open \(\operatorname{Spec}A\subset X\) one has \(\mathcal I=fA\) with \(f\) a non-zero-divisor. Over \(\operatorname{pr}^{-1}\operatorname{Spec}A=\operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_K k)\) the ideal of \(Y_k\) is \(f(A\otimes_K k)\). Since \(k\) is flat over \(K\), \(A\otimes_K k\) is flat over \(A\); tensoring the injection \(A\xrightarrow{\cdot f}A\) with the flat module \(A\otimes_K k\) shows \(f\) is still a non-zero-divisor. Hence \(Y_k\) is locally cut out by a non-zero-divisor, i.e.\(Y_k\hookrightarrow X_k\) is an effective Cartier divisor.
(c) Ample (indeed very ample). \(Y\) is very ample, so there is a closed immersion \(j:X\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_K\) with \(\mathcal O_X(Y)\cong j^*\mathcal O(1)\). Base change gives a closed immersion \(j_k:X_k\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_K\times_K k=\mathbb P^N_k\) (closed immersions are stable under base change), and the invertible ideal of \(Y_k\) is \(\operatorname{pr}^{-1}\mathcal I\otimes\mathcal O_{X_k}=\operatorname{pr}^*\mathcal I\), so \(\mathcal O_{X_k}(Y_k)=(\operatorname{pr}^*\mathcal I)^{-1}\cong\operatorname{pr}^*\mathcal O_X(Y)\cong j_k^*\mathcal O(1)\). Thus \(Y_k\) is very ample, in particular ample.
(d) Non-empty. The projection \(\operatorname{pr}_Y:Y_k\to Y\) is the base change of the surjection \(\operatorname{Spec}k\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}K\), hence surjective; \(Y\neq\varnothing\) by hypothesis, so \(Y_k\neq\varnothing\).
(e) \(Y_k\) is smooth over \(k\) (base change of the smooth \(K\)-scheme \(Y\)), hence noetherian with regular, therefore domain, local rings; it is connected because \(Y\) is geometrically connected over \(K\). By Claim 2, \(Y_k\) is integral. By Claim 1, \(\dim Y_k=\dim Y=d-1\). Hence \(Y_k\) is of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(k\).
(f) Proper inclusion. \(|Y_k|\) is closed in \(|X_k|\). If \(|Y_k|=|X_k|\), then \(\dim Y_k=\dim X_k\), i.e.\(d-1=d\), impossible (both are finite, \(d\ge2\), and \(Y_k\neq\varnothing\)). Hence \(Y_k\subsetneq X_k\).

STEP 3. Application of the geometric Lefschetz hyperplane theorem. The field \(k\) is algebraically closed and \(\ell\neq p=\operatorname{char}k\). By Steps 1 and 2, \(X_k\) is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(k\) of pure dimension \(d\ge2\), and \(Y_k\subsetneq X_k\) is a non-empty effective ample Cartier divisor, smooth of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(k\), with closed immersion \(i_k:Y_k\hookrightarrow X_k\). Lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_420 therefore applies and yields that
\[
i_k^*:H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)
\]
is an isomorphism for every integer \(m<d-1\) and injective for \(m=d-1\).

STEP 4. Conclusion. As observed at the outset, the closed immersion of the statement is precisely \(i_k\), and \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) are the étale cohomology groups of the schemes \(X_k\), \(Y_k\) (étale cohomology depends only on the underlying scheme). Taking \(m=n\) for each integer \(n\) with \(0\le n\le d-1\) gives: \(i^*\) is an isomorphism for \(n<d-1\) (this includes \(n=0\), which lies in the isomorphism range because \(d\ge2\) implies \(0<d-1\)), and \(i^*\) is injective for \(n=d-1\). This is exactly the required statement.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, \(\ell\neq p\) prime, \(m\ge1\), \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and let \(Y\subsetneq X\) be a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\), with closed immersion \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and use it to identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). For \(n\ge0\) let \(i_!:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{n+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the Gysin homomorphism. Then for every integer \(n\) with \(0\le n\le 2d-2\), the map \(i_!\) is injective if and only if \(i^*:H^{2d-n-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is surjective.
proof:
Let K = Q_l and Q = q^m. Since q is a prime power, Q is a prime power, so we may regard X and Y as varieties over F_Q. Write k = barF_q and H^r(Z) = H^r_et(Z_k, Q_l) for Z = X or Y.

First, finite dimensionality. Both X and Y are proper over F_Q: X is projective, and Y is a closed subscheme of X. The constant sheaf Q_l on Z_k has its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism. Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob with the base field F_Q in place of F_q gives that H^r(Z) is a finite-dimensional K-vector space for every r.

Fix a nonzero element e of Q_l(1) and use it to identify every Tate twist with K, as in the statement. For Z = X or Y, let tr_Z be the Poincare duality trace H^{2 dim Z}(Z_k,Q_l) -> K obtained by composing the usual trace with this identification.

For X, apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77 over F_Q. Since X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d, for every integer r with 0 <= r <= 2d the pairing <b,c>_X = tr_X(b cup c) from H^r(X) x H^{2d-r}(X) to K is perfect.

For Y, if d >= 2, then Y is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d-1 >= 1. Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77 to Y. For every integer r with 0 <= r <= 2d-2, the pairing <a,d>_Y = tr_Y(a cup d) from H^r(Y) x H^{2d-2-r}(Y) to K is perfect.
If d = 1, then the only allowed n is n = 0. In this case Y is smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension 0 over F_Q. A smooth projective zero-dimensional scheme over a field is finite etale. A finite etale scheme over F_Q is a disjoint union of spectra of finite separable extensions of F_Q; after base change to k each such spectrum of degree s splits into s copies of Spec k. Geometric connectedness therefore forces one factor of degree 1, so Y is isomorphic to Spec F_Q. Hence H^0(Y) = K and H^r(Y) = 0 for r > 0. The normalized trace tr_Y:H^0(Y) -> K sends the class of the unique closed point to its degree over F_Q, namely 1, so tr_Y(1)=1. Thus the pairing H^0(Y) x H^0(Y) -> K is perfect. This is exactly the pairing needed for r = 0.

Now fix n with 0 <= n <= 2d-2. Set A = H^n(Y), B = H^{n+2}(X), C = H^{2d-n-2}(X), D = H^{2d-n-2}(Y). Since 2d-n-2 = 2(d-1)-n, the pairings constructed above are perfect pairings A x D -> K and B x C -> K.

By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_439_gysin_projection_formula_divisor, applied over F_Q with the same identification of Tate twists, the Gysin homomorphism i_!:H^n(Y) -> H^{n+2}(X) is characterized by tr_X(i_! a cup c) = tr_Y(a cup i^* c) for all a in H^n(Y) and all c in H^{2d-2-n}(X). In the notation above this says <i_! a, c>_X = <a, i^* c>_Y for all a in A and c in C.

We now use a finite-dimensional linear algebra criterion. Let A,B,C,D be finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field K, with perfect pairings <,>_A:A x D -> K and <,>_B:B x C -> K. Let f:A -> B and g:C -> D be linear maps satisfying <f(a),c>_B = <a,g(c)>_A for all a in A and c in C. Then f is injective if and only if g is surjective. Proof: Perfectness gives dim A = dim D and dim B = dim C. Choose a basis a_1,...,a_r of A and the dual basis d_1,...,d_r of D with <a_i,d_j> = delta_ij. Choose a basis b_1,...,b_s of B and the dual basis c_1,...,c_s of C with <b_j,c_k> = delta_jk. Write f(a_i) = sum_j M_{ji} b_j and g(c_j) = sum_i N_{ij} d_i. The adjointness identity gives M_{ji} = N_{ij} for all i,j. Hence the matrix of g is the transpose of the matrix of f, so rank(g) = rank(f). Since dim A = dim D = r, f is injective iff rank(f) = r, and g is surjective iff rank(g) = r. The equivalence follows.

Apply this criterion with f = i_! and g = i^*. The adjointness identity has just been verified, and all spaces are finite-dimensional. Therefore i_!:H^n(Y) -> H^{n+2}(X) is injective if and only if i^*:H^{2d-n-2}(X) -> H^{2d-n-2}(Y) is surjective. This is exactly the desired statement for the fixed n, and n was arbitrary in the required range.

statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(Q\) be a positive rational number, let \(V\) be a nonzero finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, and let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)\). Suppose that the multiset of eigenvalues of \(T\) on \(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), counted with algebraic multiplicity, is invariant under \(\alpha\mapsto Q/\alpha\), and that there exists \(C>0\) such that for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every embedding \(\iota:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\) one has \(|\iota(\operatorname{Tr}_{V}(T^{n}))|\le C\,Q^{n/2}\). Then for every eigenvalue \(\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) of \(T\) and every embedding \(\iota:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\), \(|\iota(\alpha)|=Q^{1/2}\).
proof:
We prove the statement by pure linear algebra plus one variable complex analysis; no result from the DAG is used.

SETUP AND NOTATION. Let N = dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell} V \ge 1 (V is nonzero), and let \alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_N \in \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell be the eigenvalues of T on V \otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, listed with algebraic multiplicity. Write
  (S) the multiset \{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_N\} is invariant under \alpha \mapsto Q/\alpha,
which is a well-defined operation because T \in \mathrm{GL}(V) implies 0 is not an eigenvalue of T: indeed the characteristic polynomial of T has constant term (\pm)\det(T) \neq 0, so no eigenvalue vanishes. Hence all \alpha_i \in \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell^{\times}, and so do all Q/\alpha_i.
Put \rho := Q^{1/2} > 0 (the positive real square root), so that Q = \rho^2 and Q^{n/2} = \rho^n for every n \ge 1.

STEP 1 (power sums). Fix once and for all an embedding \iota : \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell \hookrightarrow \mathbb C. Set \beta_i := \iota(\alpha_i) \in \mathbb C^{\times}. Since \iota fixes the prime field, hence \mathbb Q pointwise, and Q \in \mathbb Q_{>0}, we have \iota(Q) = Q. It follows that the multiset \mathcal B := \{\beta_1,\dots,\beta_N\} is again invariant under \beta \mapsto Q/\beta: the map \beta \mapsto Q/\beta is the \iota-image of \alpha \mapsto Q/\alpha, and \iota is a bijection carrying the multiset \{\alpha_i\} onto \{\beta_i\} preserving multiplicities.
For m \ge 0 let p_m := \operatorname{Tr}_V(T^m) \in \mathbb Q_\ell (the trace of a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear endomorphism, with p_0 = \operatorname{Tr}_V(\mathrm{id}) = N). We claim
  \iota(p_m) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \beta_i^{m}  for every m \ge 0.   (1)
Proof of the claim: over the algebraically closed field \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell the characteristic polynomial of T \otimes \mathrm{id} splits, so T \otimes \mathrm{id} is triangularisable; choose a basis of V \otimes \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell in which its matrix is upper triangular with diagonal entries \alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_N (each appearing with its algebraic multiplicity). Then (T\otimes\mathrm{id})^m = (T\otimes\mathrm{id})^m is upper triangular with diagonal entries \alpha_1^m,\dots,\alpha_N^m, so \operatorname{Tr}(T^m \otimes \mathrm{id}) = \sum_i \alpha_i^m. Trace is unchanged by the faithfully flat base change \mathbb Q_\ell \to \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, so p_m = \sum_i \alpha_i^m in \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, and applying the field homomorphism \iota gives (1).

STEP 2 (the generating function is a SUM of geometric series). Group the distinct values among the \beta_i as \gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_t (t \ge 1, each \gamma_j \neq 0) with multiplicities m_1,\dots,m_t \ge 1, so that \sum_j m_j = N and, by (1),
  \iota(p_m) = \sum_{j=1}^{t} m_j \gamma_j^{m}.   (2)
Define polynomials
  D(z) := \prod_{j=1}^{t} (1 - \gamma_j z), \qquad N(z) := \sum_{j=1}^{t} m_j \prod_{k\neq j} (1 - \gamma_k z).
Since the \gamma_j are pairwise distinct, D has only simple zeros, and putting the partial-fraction sum over the common denominator D gives the identity of rational functions
  \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{1}{1-\beta_i z} = \sum_{j=1}^{t} \frac{m_j}{1-\gamma_j z} = \frac{N(z)}{D(z)}.   (3)
Non-vanishing at the candidate poles. For each j,
  N(\gamma_j^{-1}) = m_j \prod_{k\neq j}\Bigl(1 - \frac{\gamma_k}{\gamma_j}\Bigr) \neq 0,   (4)
because m_j \ge 1 is a nonzero integer in \mathbb C, and \gamma_k \neq \gamma_j for k \neq j makes each factor 1-\gamma_k/\gamma_j nonzero (all \gamma_k are nonzero). (Equivalently: in the sum defining N, every summand with index j' \neq j contains the factor (1-\gamma_j z), which vanishes at z = \gamma_j^{-1}.)

STEP 3 (analytic continuation and the pole argument). Define
  R_c := \Bigl(\limsup_{m\to\infty} |\iota(p_m)|^{1/m}\Bigr)^{-1} \in (0,+\infty].
By hypothesis (B) applied to the chosen \iota, |\iota(p_m)| \le C \rho^m for all m \ge 1, whence \limsup_m |\iota(p_m)|^{1/m} \le \rho \cdot \lim_m C^{1/m} = \rho, so
  R_c \ge 1/\rho.   (5)
By the Cauchy--Hadamard theorem the power series f(z) := \sum_{m\ge 0} \iota(p_m) z^m converges absolutely, and defines a holomorphic function, on the disc \{|z| < R_c\}.
Let r_0 := \min_{1\le j\le t} |\gamma_j|^{-1} > 0 (a minimum over a nonempty finite set of positive reals). For |z| < r_0 each geometric series \sum_{m\ge 0}(\beta_i z)^m converges absolutely to (1-\beta_i z)^{-1}; since the sum over i is finite, we may interchange the order of summation:
  f(z) = \sum_{m\ge 0}\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\beta_i^{m}\Bigr) z^{m} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{m\ge 0}(\beta_i z)^{m} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{1-\beta_i z} = \frac{N(z)}{D(z)}, \qquad |z| < r_0,
where the first equality uses (1) and the last is (3). Hence
  f(z) D(z) = N(z) \quad\text{for all } |z| < r_0.   (6)
Now consider g(z) := f(z)D(z) - N(z). The function g is holomorphic on the whole disc \{|z| < R_c\} (f is holomorphic there by Cauchy--Hadamard; D and N are polynomials). The set U := \{z : |z| < \min(r_0, R_c)\} is a nonempty open disc (its radius is positive) contained in \{|z|<R_c\}, and g vanishes on U by (6). The disc \{|z|<R_c\} is open and connected, and U has an accumulation point in it, so the identity theorem gives
  f(z) D(z) = N(z) \quad\text{for all } |z| < R_c.   (7)
Suppose, for a contradiction, that some |\beta_i| > \rho; say |\gamma_{j_0}| > \rho for some j_0. Put z_0 := \gamma_{j_0}^{-1}. Then 0 < |z_0| = 1/|\gamma_{j_0}| < 1/\rho \le R_c by (5), so z_0 lies in the disc of holomorphy of g, and (7) applies at z_0. But D(z_0) = 0 because the factor k = j_0 of D vanishes at z_0. Therefore (7) yields 0 = f(z_0)\cdot 0 = N(z_0) = N(\gamma_{j_0}^{-1}), contradicting the non-vanishing (4). We conclude
  |\beta_i| \le \rho \quad\text{for every } i = 1,\dots,N.   (8)

STEP 4 (the reciprocal symmetry gives the reverse inequality). By Step 1 the multiset \mathcal B is invariant under the involution \beta \mapsto Q/\beta of \mathbb C^{\times}. Hence there exists a permutation \sigma of \{1,\dots,N\} such that
  \beta_i = Q/\beta_{\sigma(i)} \quad\text{for all } i,
for instance: invariance of the multiset means the assignment i \mapsto (the index of Q/\beta_i) can be made a bijection, since the map \beta\mapsto Q/\beta is a bijection of \mathbb C^{\times} sending \mathcal B onto itself with the same multiplicities. Taking moduli,
  |\beta_{\sigma(i)}| = Q/|\beta_i| = \rho^{2}/|\beta_i|.
Applying the upper bound (8) to the index \sigma(i) (which is legitimate because \sigma is a bijection, so \sigma(i) runs through all indices as i does) gives \rho^{2}/|\beta_i| \le \rho, and since \rho > 0 and |\beta_i| > 0 this is equivalent to
  |\beta_i| \ge \rho \quad\text{for every } i.   (9)
Combining (8) and (9) we obtain |\beta_i| = \rho = Q^{1/2} for every i.

STEP 5 (removal of the choice of \iota). The embedding \iota was fixed arbitrarily at the start of Step 1 and never otherwise constrained; the hypotheses (S) and (B) are stated for the multiset of eigenvalues and for every embedding, so the argument applies verbatim to any \iota. Hence for every eigenvalue \alpha of T and every embedding \iota : \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell \hookrightarrow \mathbb C we have |\iota(\alpha)| = \rho = Q^{1/2}, which is the desired conclusion.

REMARKS ON THE USE OF THE HYPOTHESES. The invertibility of T was used only to ensure \alpha_i \neq 0, so that both Q/\alpha_i and \gamma_j^{-1} are defined; hypothesis (B) was used exactly once, in (5), to make the radius of convergence of \sum_m \iota(p_m)z^m at least 1/\rho, so that the genuine poles \gamma_j^{-1} of the rational function N/D forced by (4) fall inside the disc where the identity fD = N holds; hypothesis (S) was used exactly once, in Step 4. The constant C is permitted to depend on everything except m, and only its m-independence entered, through C^{1/m} \to 1. No claim was made about algebraicity of the eigenvalues over \mathbb Q, and no generating function other than the sum \sum_i (1-\beta_i z)^{-1} was used.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(X\) be a proper variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and let \(F_X:X_k\to X_k\) be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius. Let \(K\) be a semisimple perverse \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\)-sheaf on \(X_k\) for the middle perversity and let \(\varphi:F_X^*K\xrightarrow{\sim}K\) be an isomorphism. Let \(L\) be an absolutely simple perverse subsheaf of \(K\), let \(d\ge1\) be minimal such that \(F_X^{d*}L\cong L\), and let \(K_L\) be the sum of all simple subsheaves of \(K\) isomorphic to \(F_X^{j*}L\) for some \(0\le j<d\). Then the natural evaluation map \[\bigoplus_{j=0}^{d-1} F_X^{j*}L\otimes_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{Perv}(X_k,\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)}(F_X^{j*}L,K_L)\to K_L\] is an isomorphism.
proof:
Proof. Let Perv denote the Qbar_l-linear abelian category of constructible perverse sheaves on X_k. Put L_j = F_X^{j*}L for 0 <= j < d. The q-power arithmetic Frobenius F_X is an automorphism of X_k; pullback by F_X is an exact autoequivalence of Perv, hence preserves simple objects.

Since K is semisimple in the finite-length category of constructible perverse sheaves, it is a finite direct sum of simple objects; write K = direct sum_{a=1}^N S_a. (This is the usual definition of a semisimple object in this setting and is the hypothesis needed to apply lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_20.)

We first record Schur's lemma. If A and B are simple objects of Perv and f:A -> B is nonzero, then ker(f) is a subobject of A and coker(f) is a quotient of B; simplicity forces ker(f)=0 and coker(f)=0, so f is an isomorphism. Consequently Hom(A,B)=0 when A and B are non-isomorphic, and End(A) is a division ring.

First, every L_j occurs in K. The inclusion L_0 = L subset K is given. If L_j subset K, then exactness of F_X^* gives F_X^*L_j subset F_X^*K, and phi maps this subobject isomorphically onto a subobject of K isomorphic to F_X^*L_j = L_{j+1}. Thus all L_j occur as simple subsheaves of K. If L_i is isomorphic to L_j with i < j, applying (F_X^i)^{-1*} gives L isomorphic to F_X^{(j-i)*}L with 0 < j-i < d, contradicting minimality of d. Hence L_0,...,L_{d-1} are pairwise non-isomorphic. Also F_X^{t*}L is isomorphic to L_r where r is the residue of t modulo d.

For each j define K_{L,j} to be the sum of all simple subobjects of K_L isomorphic to L_j. In the decomposition K = direct sum_{a=1}^N S_a, let C_j be the direct sum of those S_a which are isomorphic to L_j. Each summand S_a of C_j is a simple subobject of K isomorphic to L_j, hence is contained in K_{L,j}; therefore C_j subset K_{L,j}. Conversely, let M subset K be simple and isomorphic to L_j. For each a, the projection p_a:M -> S_a is either zero or an isomorphism. If p_a is nonzero, then by Schur's lemma S_a is isomorphic to M and hence to L_j, so S_a is a summand of C_j. Since K is the direct sum of the S_a, M is contained in C_j. Therefore K_{L,j}=C_j. In particular K_{L,j} is isomorphic to L_j^{oplus m_j} for some finite integer m_j, and K_L = direct sum_{j=0}^{d-1} K_{L,j}.

We next compute endomorphism algebras. Since K is a finite direct sum of simple perverse sheaves and phi:F_X^*K -> K is a Frobenius isomorphism, lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_20 implies that Ext^n_{D^b_c}(K,K) is finite-dimensional over Qbar_l for every n. For n=0, Hom_{Perv}(K,K)=Hom_{D^b_c}(K,K)=Ext^0_{D^b_c}(K,K), so End(K) is finite-dimensional. Each L_j is a direct summand of K; choose an inclusion i_j:L_j -> K and a retraction p_j:K -> L_j. The map End(L_j) -> End(K), u -> i_j u p_j, is injective because p_j(i_j u p_j)i_j = u. Thus End(L_j) is finite-dimensional over Qbar_l.

Since End(L_j) is a finite-dimensional division algebra over the algebraically closed field Qbar_l, it equals Qbar_l. Indeed, for u in End(L_j), the Qbar_l-subalgebra Qbar_l[u] is finite-dimensional, commutative, and has no zero divisors. A finite-dimensional commutative domain over a field is a field: multiplication by a nonzero element is injective and hence surjective. Therefore Qbar_l[u] is a finite field extension of Qbar_l, hence Qbar_l[u]=Qbar_l, so u is scalar. Thus End(L_j)=Qbar_l.

Now fix j and r. Since K_{L,r} is a finite direct sum of copies of L_r and L_j is not isomorphic to L_r for r != j, Schur's lemma gives Hom(L_j,K_{L,r})=0 for r != j. Because K_L is the finite direct sum of the K_{L,r}, Hom(L_j,K_L) = direct sum_{r=0}^{d-1} Hom(L_j,K_{L,r}) = Hom(L_j,K_{L,j}).

It remains to prove that the evaluation map on K_{L,j} is an isomorphism. Choose an isomorphism alpha:L_j^{oplus m_j} -> K_{L,j}. Let i_a:L_j -> L_j^{oplus m_j} be the a-th inclusion and p_a the a-th projection, 1 <= a <= m_j. Put f_a = alpha i_a in Hom(L_j,K_{L,j}). For any f in Hom(L_j,K_{L,j}), alpha^{-1}f has components p_a alpha^{-1}f in End(L_j)=Qbar_l, so f = sum_a c_a f_a for unique c_a in Qbar_l. Hence f_1,...,f_{m_j} is a Qbar_l-basis of Hom(L_j,K_{L,j}). The evaluation map ev_j:L_j tensor Hom(L_j,K_{L,j}) -> K_{L,j}, s tensor f -> f(s), sends sum_a s_a tensor f_a to alpha(s_1,...,s_{m_j}). Therefore, under the canonical identification L_j tensor Hom(L_j,K_{L,j}) = L_j tensor Qbar_l^{m_j} = L_j^{oplus m_j}, ev_j is alpha composed with the identity. Hence ev_j is an isomorphism.

Finally, the map in the statement is the direct sum over j of the component maps L_j tensor Hom(L_j,K_L) -> K_{L,j} followed by the inclusion K_{L,j} -> K_L. By the orthogonality just proved, Hom(L_j,K_L)=Hom(L_j,K_{L,j}), and these component maps are exactly the isomorphisms ev_j. A direct sum of isomorphisms is an isomorphism. This proves the required evaluation map is an isomorphism. QED.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(m\ge1\), and let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Then there exist an integer \(m'\) divisible by \(m\), a closed immersion \(X_{\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}}\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}}\) for some \(N\), and \(\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}\)-rational hyperplanes \(H_1,\dots,H_d\) such that, writing \(X_j=X_{\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}}\cap H_1\cap\cdots\cap H_j\) (with \(X_0=X_{\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}}\)), each \(X_j\) for \(0\le j\le d-1\) is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-j\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}\), and \(X_d\) is a nonempty finite etale \(\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}\)-scheme.
proof:
Let k0=F_{q^m}. Since X is projective over k0, choose a closed immersion i0: X -> P^N_{k0}. If one defines projective via an ample line bundle, take a sufficiently high very ample tensor power of an ample line bundle to obtain such a closed immersion. We split into the cases d=1 and d>=2.

Case d=1. Apply Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/94e8aa to the closed subscheme Y=X of P^N_{F_{q^m}} with e=1. The lemma gives a finite extension K/F_{q^m} and a K-rational hyperplane H1 such that X1=X_K cap H1 is nonempty, smooth, and pure of dimension 0 over K. Every finite extension of F_{q^m} is of the form F_{q^{mt}} for some t>=1; write K=F_{q^{mt}} and set m'=mt. Then m' is divisible by m. Base changing i0 gives a closed immersion X_{F_{q^{m'}}} -> P^N_{F_{q^{m'}}}. The hyperplane H1 is defined over K=F_{q^{m'}}, hence is an F_{q^{m'}}-rational hyperplane. Also X0=X_{F_{q^{m'}}} is smooth, geometrically connected, and pure of dimension 1 over F_{q^{m'}}, because these properties are stable under extension of the base field. Finally X1=X_{F_{q^{m'}}} cap H1 is nonempty, smooth, and pure of dimension 0 over F_{q^{m'}}.

Case d>=2. Apply Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/4f6e82 to the closed subscheme X of P^N_{F_{q^m}}. It gives an integer r>=1 divisible by m and F_{q^r}-rational hyperplanes H1,...,H_{d-1} such that, for each 1<=j<=d-1, the scheme-theoretic intersection X_j=X_{F_{q^r}} cap H1 cap ... cap Hj is smooth, geometrically connected, and pure of dimension d-j over F_{q^r}. In particular X_{d-1} is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_{q^r}, and it is a closed subscheme of P^N_{F_{q^r}}. Apply Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/94e8aa to Y=X_{d-1} over F_{q^r} with e=1. It gives a finite extension K/F_{q^r} and a K-rational hyperplane Hd such that X_d=(X_{d-1})_K cap Hd is nonempty, smooth, and pure of dimension 0 over K. Write K=F_{q^{rt}} for some t>=1 and set m'=rt. Since r is divisible by m, m' is divisible by m. View H1,...,Hd as hyperplanes over F_{q^{m'}}. Base changing i0 gives a closed immersion X_{F_{q^{m'}}} -> P^N_{F_{q^{m'}}}. For each 0<=j<=d-1, the scheme X_j defined by intersecting X_{F_{q^{m'}}} with H1,...,Hj is the base change to F_{q^{m'}} of the corresponding scheme over F_{q^r} (for j=0 this is just X_{F_{q^{m'}}}, obtained from X over F_{q^m} by first extending scalars to F_{q^r} and then to F_{q^{m'}}). Smoothness, pure dimension, and geometric connectedness are stable under extension of the base field, so each X_j is smooth, geometrically connected, and pure of dimension d-j over F_{q^{m'}}. Moreover X_d=(X_{F_{q^{m'}}}) cap H1 cap ... cap Hd is nonempty, smooth, and pure of dimension 0 over F_{q^{m'}}.

It remains to prove that X_d is finite etale over F_{q^{m'}}. Put k'=F_{q^{m'}} and S=X_d. The scheme S is a closed subscheme of P^N_{k'}, hence of finite type over the field k'. It is smooth over k' and pure of dimension 0. Smoothness over a field implies etaleness. Since S has finite type over k' and dimension 0, every affine open Spec A of S is a noetherian ring of Krull dimension 0, hence Artinian. Smoothness implies A is regular, and a regular noetherian local ring of dimension 0 is a field; thus A is a finite product of fields. Each field factor is a finitely generated k'-algebra, hence a finite field extension of k' by the standard Zariski lemma for finitely generated fields over a field. Smoothness over k' forces these finite extensions to be separable. Therefore S is a finite disjoint union of spectra of finite separable field extensions of k', i.e. a finite etale k'-scheme. Nonemptiness of S was supplied by Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/94e8aa. This completes the proof.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimensions \(d\) and \(e\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(\xi_X\) and \(\xi_Y\) be the cycle classes of \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-rational very ample divisors on \(X\) and \(Y\), and let \(L_X\), \(L_Y\), and \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi_X\), with \(\xi_Y\), and with \(\operatorname{pr}_1^*\xi_X+\operatorname{pr}_2^*\xi_Y\). Suppose \(L_X^{d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(L_Y^{e-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2e-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) are isomorphisms for every \(0\le n\le d\) and every \(0\le n\le e\). Then \(L^{d+e-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d+2e-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le n\le d+e\).
proof:
We write $Q:=q^{m}=p^{am}$, which is again a prime power, so that $X$ and $Y$ are smooth projective geometrically connected varieties over $\mathbb F_{Q}$ and $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q}=\overline{\mathbb F}_{Q}$. Throughout, $H^*(-)$ means $H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(-,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, and the fixed nonzero element of $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ is used to identify Tate twists with $\mathbb Q_\ell$, so that cycle classes of codimension-one cycles lie in $H^2$.

**Step 0: Notation and the two graded spaces.** Put
\[
V:=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}V_r,\qquad V_r:=H^r(X_k),\qquad W:=\bigoplus_{s\ge0}W_s,\qquad W_s:=H^s(Y_k),
\]
and let $L_V:=L_X$ (cup product with $\xi_X$) and $L_W:=L_Y$ (cup product with $\xi_Y$). Let $Z:=X\times_{\mathbb F_{Q}}Y$, let $\pi_i:Z_k\to X_k$ (resp. $Y_k$) be the base change of $\operatorname{pr}_i$, and put $\eta:=\pi_1^*\xi_X+\pi_2^*\xi_Y\in H^2(Z_k)$; then $L$ is cup product with $\eta$.

*Finite dimensionality.* $X$ and $Y$ are proper over $\mathbb F_Q$, and the constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$ on $X_k$ (resp. $Y_k$) carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism, so by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob each $H^n(X_k)$ and $H^n(Y_k)$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$.

*Support of the grading.* $X_k$ (resp. $Y_k$) is projective over the algebraically closed field $k$ and, being the base change of a smooth $\mathbb F_Q$-scheme of pure dimension $d$ (resp. $e$), it is smooth of relative dimension $d$ (resp. $e$) over $k$; hence it is equidimensional of dimension $d$ (resp. $e$). Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_projective_cohomology_vanishes_above_twice_dimension with $n=d$ (resp. $n=e$) gives $V_r=0$ for all $r>2d$ and $W_s=0$ for all $s>2e$. Etale cohomology also vanishes in negative degrees. Hence
\[
V=\bigoplus_{r=0}^{2d}V_r,\qquad W=\bigoplus_{s=0}^{2e}W_s
\]
as $\mathbb Z$-graded $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces, each piece finite-dimensional.

*Degree behaviour of $L_V,L_W$.* Cup product with a class of degree $2$ sends $H^r$ to $H^{r+2}$; since $\xi_X\in H^2(X_k)$ and $\xi_Y\in H^2(Y_k)$, we have $L_V(V_r)\subseteq V_{r+2}$ and $L_W(W_s)\subseteq W_{s+2}$.

**Step 1: The K\"unneth identification.** Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_146 to the prime power $Q$ and the smooth projective $\mathbb F_Q$-varieties $X,Y$: for every $t\ge0$ the map
\[
\kappa_t:\bigoplus_{r+s=t}V_r\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}W_s\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\;H^t(Z_k),\qquad x\otimes y\longmapsto \pi_1^*x\cup\pi_2^*y,
\]
is an isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces. Collecting the $\kappa_t$ gives a graded isomorphism $\kappa:V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}W\xrightarrow{\sim}H^*(Z_k)$ identifying the tensor-product grading $(V\otimes W)_t=\bigoplus_{r+s=t}V_r\otimes W_s$ with $H^t(Z_k)$.

**Step 2: Intertwining $L$ with $L_V\otimes\mathrm{id}+\mathrm{id}\otimes L_W$.** We check on simple tensors of homogeneous elements. Let $x\in V_r$, $y\in W_s$. Using: (i) bilinearity and distributivity of the cup product; (ii) functoriality of pull-back, $\pi_i^*(a\cup b)=\pi_i^*a\cup\pi_i^*b$; (iii) associativity; and (iv) graded commutativity $a\cup b=(-1)^{\deg a\,\deg b}b\cup a$, applied only to the class $\pi_2^*\xi_Y$ of degree $2$ (and symmetrically to $\pi_1^*\xi_X$), so that no sign appears, we compute:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\kappa\bigl((L_V\otimes\mathrm{id}+\mathrm{id}\otimes L_W)(x\otimes y)\bigr)
&=\kappa(L_Vx\otimes y)+\kappa(x\otimes L_Wy)\\
&=\bigl(\pi_1^*(\xi_X\cup x)\bigr)\cup\pi_2^*y\;+\;\pi_1^*x\cup\bigl(\pi_2^*(\xi_Y\cup y)\bigr)\\
&=\bigl(\pi_1^*\xi_X\cup\pi_1^*x\bigr)\cup\pi_2^*y\;+\;\pi_1^*x\cup\bigl(\pi_2^*\xi_Y\cup\pi_2^*y\bigr)\\
&=\pi_1^*\xi_X\cup\bigl(\pi_1^*x\cup\pi_2^*y\bigr)\;+\;\pi_2^*\xi_Y\cup\bigl(\pi_1^*x\cup\pi_2^*y\bigr)\\
&=\bigl(\pi_1^*\xi_X+\pi_2^*\xi_Y\bigr)\cup\kappa(x\otimes y)=\eta\cup\kappa(x\otimes y)=L\bigl(\kappa(x\otimes y)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
In the third line we used associativity together with graded commutativity to move $\pi_1^*\xi_X$ (degree $2$) past $\pi_1^*x$ (degree $r$) and $\pi_2^*\xi_Y$ (degree $2$) past $\pi_1^*x$ (degree $r$); the signs are $(-1)^{2r}=+1$ in both cases. Both $\kappa\circ(L_V\otimes\mathrm{id}+\mathrm{id}\otimes L_W)$ and $L\circ\kappa$ are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear maps on $\bigoplus_{r+s=t}V_r\otimes W_s$ that agree on the spanning set of simple tensors of homogeneous elements; hence
\[
L\circ\kappa_t=\kappa_t\circ\bigl(L_V\otimes\mathrm{id}+\mathrm{id}\otimes L_W\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0.
\]
By induction on $N$, using that $\kappa$ is graded and the identity above in each degree, $(L_V\otimes\mathrm{id}+\mathrm{id}\otimes L_W)^N$ maps $(V\otimes W)_t$ into $(V\otimes W)_{t+2N}$ and
\[
\kappa_{t+2N}\circ\bigl(L_V\otimes\mathrm{id}+\mathrm{id}\otimes L_W\bigr)^{N}=L^{N}\circ\kappa_t .
\tag{$\ast$}
\]

**Step 3: The hard Lefschetz hypotheses on $V$ and $W$.** By assumption, $L_X^{\,d-n}:H^n(X_k)\to H^{2d-n}(X_k)$ is an isomorphism for every $0\le n\le d$, i.e. $L_V^{\,d-n}:V_n\to V_{2d-n}$ is an isomorphism for every $0\le n\le d$; and $L_Y^{\,e-n}:W_n\to W_{2e-n}$ is an isomorphism for every $0\le n\le e$. These are exactly the hypotheses of Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_tensor_product_lefschetz with $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ (a field of characteristic $0$), $m=d$, $n=e$, together with the grading/support and degree-raising properties established in Step 0.

**Step 4: Apply the tensor-product Lefschetz lemma.** That lemma yields, for every $0\le t\le d+e$, that
\[
\bigl(L_V\otimes\mathrm{id}_W+\mathrm{id}_V\otimes L_W\bigr)^{d+e-t}:(V\otimes W)_t\longrightarrow (V\otimes W)_{2d+2e-t}
\]
is an isomorphism. (The exponent is $\ge0$ because $t\le d+e$.) Via the graded isomorphism $\kappa$, $(V\otimes W)_t\simeq H^t(Z_k)$ and $(V\otimes W)_{2d+2e-t}\simeq H^{2d+2e-t}(Z_k)$. By $(\ast)$ with $N=d+e-t$, the operator $L^{\,d+e-t}:H^t(Z_k)\to H^{2d+2e-t}(Z_k)$ is the transport along $\kappa$ of an isomorphism, hence itself an isomorphism. Since $t$ was arbitrary in $[0,d+e]$, this is precisely the required conclusion.

**Step 5: Degenerate dimensions.** The argument above is uniform, but we record the edge cases explicitly. If $d=0$, then $X$ is proper, smooth and geometrically connected of dimension $0$ over $\mathbb F_Q$, hence $X\simeq\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_Q$; then $H^2(X_k)=0$ by Step 0 (vanishing above twice the dimension), so $\xi_X=0$, $L_V=0$, and $L=\mathrm{id}\otimes L_Y$ under $\kappa$. The hypothesis on $X$ is then vacuous (it only asserts $L_V^0=\mathrm{id}:V_0\to V_0$ is an isomorphism), and Step 4 with $m=0$ is exactly the assumed hard Lefschetz statement for $Y$; the same holds symmetrically when $e=0$, and when $d=e=0$ both sides reduce to $\mathrm{id}:\mathbb Q_\ell\to\mathbb Q_\ell$. No separate construction is needed.

Thus $L^{\,d+e-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d+2e-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is an isomorphism for every $0\le n\le d+e$. $\blacksquare$

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(m\ge1\), let \(d\ge2\), and let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Let \(\mathcal L\) be a very ample line bundle on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Then there exist an integer \(m'\ge1\) divisible by \(m\), an integer \(n\ge1\), and a section \(s\in H^0(X_{\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}},\mathcal L^{\otimes n})\) whose zero scheme \(Y=V(s)\) is a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor on \(X_{\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}}\), smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}\).
proof: Let K = F_{q^m}. Since L is very ample over K, there exists an integer n >= 1 and a closed immersion phi: X -> P^N_K such that phi^* O_{P^N}(1) is isomorphic to L^{tensor n}. (If very ample is taken in the usual sense, one may take n = 1; the argument is unchanged if a positive tensor power is used.) Identify X with its image under phi. Then X is a smooth projective geometrically connected closed subscheme of P^N_K of pure dimension d. Apply lemma Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/4f6e82 to this closed subscheme. It gives an integer m' >= 1 divisible by m and hyperplanes H_1,...,H_{d-1} in P^N_{F_{q^{m'}}}, all defined over F_{q^{m'}}, such that X_1 := X_{F_{q^{m'}}} cap H_1 is smooth, geometrically connected, and of pure dimension d-1 over F_{q^{m'}}. Let s_H be the canonical section of O_{P^N}(1) whose zero scheme is H_1, and let s be the pullback of s_H to X_{F_{q^{m'}}} via the base change of phi. Under the identification phi^* O_{P^N}(1) = L^{tensor n}, this gives s in H^0(X_{F_{q^{m'}}}, L^{tensor n}). The zero scheme of s is exactly the scheme-theoretic intersection Y := X_{F_{q^{m'}}} cap H_1 = X_1. Since d >= 2, Y has pure dimension d-1 >= 1, so Y is nonempty. The scheme X_{F_{q^{m'}}} is smooth and geometrically connected over F_{q^{m'}}; hence it is connected and regular. A connected regular noetherian scheme is integral, so X_{F_{q^{m'}}} is integral. The hyperplane H_1 does not contain X_{F_{q^{m'}}}, because otherwise X_1 would have dimension d, contradicting that it has pure dimension d-1. Therefore the section s is not identically zero. On an integral scheme, every nonzero local function is a nonzerodivisor; consequently the zero scheme of a nonzero section of a line bundle is an effective Cartier divisor. Thus Y is an effective Cartier divisor on X_{F_{q^{m'}}}. Its associated line bundle is O(Y) = L^{tensor n}_{F_{q^{m'}}}, which is very ample as the base change of the very ample line bundle L^{tensor n}. Hence Y is a very ample Cartier divisor. The smoothness and geometric connectedness of Y are exactly the properties of X_1 supplied by lemma Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/4f6e82. This completes the proof.

statement: Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic \(0\), let \(V\) be a \(4\)-dimensional \(K\)-vector space, let \(\operatorname{vol}:\textstyle\bigwedge^{4}_{K}V\to K\) be a nonzero \(K\)-linear map, and let \(\omega\in\bigwedge^{2}_{K}V\). Then the bilinear form \((u,v)\mapsto\operatorname{vol}(\omega\wedge u\wedge v)\) on \(V\) is nondegenerate if and only if \(\operatorname{vol}(\omega\wedge\omega)\neq 0\).
proof:
We prove the equivalence by an explicit computation in a suitably normalised basis. No geometric input is needed; the argument is pure linear algebra over the characteristic-0 field $K$.

STEP 0. Preliminaries on $\operatorname{vol}$ and on the form $B$.
Since $\dim_K V=4$, $\bigwedge^4_K V$ is $1$-dimensional: for any $K$-basis $f_1,\dots,f_4$ of $V$, the element $f_1\wedge f_2\wedge f_3\wedge f_4$ is a basis of $\bigwedge^4_K V$. A $K$-linear map $\operatorname{vol}:\bigwedge^4_K V\to K$ that is nonzero therefore does not vanish on that basis vector (otherwise it would vanish on all of $\bigwedge^4_K V$, as every element is a scalar multiple of it), and hence $\operatorname{vol}$ is an isomorphism.

Define $B:V\times V\to K$ by $B(u,v)=\operatorname{vol}(\omega\wedge u\wedge v)$. Bilinearity of $B$ follows from bilinearity of the wedge product and $K$-linearity of $\operatorname{vol}$. Moreover $B$ is alternating: $B(v,v)=\operatorname{vol}(\omega\wedge v\wedge v)=0$ because $v\wedge v=0$ in the exterior algebra, and $B(v,u)=\operatorname{vol}(\omega\wedge v\wedge u)=-\operatorname{vol}(\omega\wedge u\wedge v)=-B(u,v)$ because $v\wedge u=-u\wedge v$. (Equivalently, $B$ is the alternating form whose class in $\bigwedge^2 V^*$ corresponds to $\omega$ under $\bigwedge^2 V\xrightarrow{\sim}\bigwedge^2 V^*\otimes\bigwedge^4 V\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}\otimes\operatorname{vol}}\bigwedge^2 V^*$.)

STEP 1. Choice of a normalised basis.
Pick any basis $f_1,\dots,f_4$ of $V$ and put $c=\operatorname{vol}(f_1\wedge f_2\wedge f_3\wedge f_4)\in K^\times$ by Step 0. Then $e_1=c^{-1}f_1$, $e_2=f_2$, $e_3=f_3$, $e_4=f_4$ is again a basis and satisfies
$$\operatorname{vol}(e_1\wedge e_2\wedge e_3\wedge e_4)=c^{-1}\operatorname{vol}(f_1\wedge f_2\wedge f_3\wedge f_4)=1.$$
Write $E=e_1\wedge e_2\wedge e_3\wedge e_4$, so $\operatorname{vol}(E)=1$. We shall compute both sides of the claimed equivalence in this basis.

STEP 2. Coordinates of $\omega$ and of $B$.
Write uniquely
$$\omega=\sum_{1\le i<j\le 4} a_{ij}\, e_i\wedge e_j,\qquad a_{ij}\in K.$$
For a strictly increasing pair $i<j$ let $\{k,l\}=\{1,2,3,4\}\setminus\{i,j\}$ with $k<l$. Expanding,
$$B(e_i,e_j)=\operatorname{vol}(\omega\wedge e_i\wedge e_j)=\sum_{p<q} a_{pq}\,\operatorname{vol}(e_p\wedge e_q\wedge e_i\wedge e_j).$$
If $\{p,q\}\cap\{i,j\}\ne\varnothing$ then some $e_r$ with $r\in\{i,j\}$ occurs twice in $e_p\wedge e_q\wedge e_i\wedge e_j$, so that term is $0$. If $\{p,q\}=\{k,l\}$ then, since the $e_1,\dots,e_4$ anticommute pairwise and square to zero, $e_p\wedge e_q\wedge e_i\wedge e_j=\operatorname{sgn}(p,q,i,j)\,E$, where $\operatorname{sgn}(p,q,i,j)$ is the sign of the permutation taking the ordered quadruple $(p,q,i,j)$ to $(1,2,3,4)$, i.e. $(-1)^{N}$ with $N$ the number of inversions of the sequence $(p,q,i,j)$. Hence $B(e_i,e_j)=\operatorname{sgn}(k,l,i,j)\,a_{kl}$. Computing the six signs by counting inversions:
\begin{itemize}
\item $(i,j)=(1,2)$: $(k,l,i,j)=(3,4,1,2)$, inversions $(3,1),(3,2),(4,1),(4,2)$: $N=4$, sign $+1$, so $B(e_1,e_2)=a_{34}$.
\item $(i,j)=(1,3)$: $(2,4,1,3)$, inversions $(2,1),(4,1),(4,3)$: $N=3$, sign $-1$, so $B(e_1,e_3)=-a_{24}$.
\item $(i,j)=(1,4)$: $(2,3,1,4)$, inversions $(2,1),(3,1)$: $N=2$, sign $+1$, so $B(e_1,e_4)=a_{23}$.
\item $(i,j)=(2,3)$: $(1,4,2,3)$, inversions $(4,2),(4,3)$: $N=2$, sign $+1$, so $B(e_2,e_3)=a_{14}$.
\item $(i,j)=(2,4)$: $(1,3,2,4)$, inversions $(3,2)$: $N=1$, sign $-1$, so $B(e_2,e_4)=-a_{13}$.
\item $(i,j)=(3,4)$: $(1,2,3,4)$, $N=0$, sign $+1$, so $B(e_3,e_4)=a_{12}$.
\end{itemize}
Writing $M_{ij}:=B(e_i,e_j)$ for $i<j$, and using $M_{ii}=0$, $M_{ji}=-M_{ij}$ (Step 0), the matrix of $B$ in the basis $(e_i)$ is
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&M_{12}&M_{13}&M_{14\\}-M_{12}&0&M_{23}&M_{24}\\-M_{13}&-M_{23}&0&M_{34}\\-M_{14}&-M_{24}&-M_{34}&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\text{with}\quad\begin{aligned} M_{12}&=a_{34},\\ M_{13}&=-a_{24},\quad M_{23}=a_{14},\\ M_{14}&=a_{23},\quad M_{24}=-a_{13},\\ M_{34}&=a_{12}.\end{aligned}$$

STEP 3. Determinant of a $4\times4$ alternating matrix (Pfaffian formula), proved by direct expansion.
Put $a=M_{12}$, $b=M_{13}$, $c=M_{14}$, $d=M_{23}$, $e=M_{24}$, $f=M_{34}$, so
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&a&b&c\\-a&0&d&e\\-b&-d&0&f\\-c&-e&-f&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Expanding along the first row, $\det A=-a\det A_{12}+b\det A_{13}-c\det A_{14}$, where $A_{1j}$ is the minor obtained by deleting row $1$ and column $j$.
\begin{itemize}
\item $A_{12}=\begin{pmatrix}-a&d&e\\-b&0&f\\-c&-f&0\end{pmatrix}$, so $\det A_{12}=-a(0\cdot 0-f(-f))-d((-b)\cdot 0-f(-c))+e((-b)(-f)-0(-c))=-af^{2}-cdf+bef$.
\item $A_{13}=\begin{pmatrix}-a&0&e\\-b&-d&f\\-c&-e&0\end{pmatrix}$, so $\det A_{13}=-a((-d)\cdot 0-f(-e))-0+e((-b)(-e)-(-d)(-c))=-aef+be^{2}-cde$.
\item $A_{14}=\begin{pmatrix}-a&0&d\\-b&-d&0\\-c&-e&-f\end{pmatrix}$, so $\det A_{14}=-a((-d)(-f)-0(-e))-0+d((-b)(-e)-(-d)(-c))=-adf+bde-cd^{2}$.
\end{itemize}
Therefore
$$\det A=\bigl(a^{2}f^{2}+acdf-abef\bigr)+\bigl(-abef+b^{2}e^{2}-bcde\bigr)+\bigl(acdf-bcde+c^{2}d^{2}\bigr)$$
$$=a^{2}f^{2}+b^{2}e^{2}+c^{2}d^{2}+2acdf-2abef-2bcde=(af-be+cd)^{2},$$
where the last identity is the literal expansion of $(af-be+cd)^2=a^2f^2+b^2e^2+c^2d^2-2abef+2acdf-2bcde$. Thus, with $M$'s,
$$\det A=\bigl(M_{12}M_{34}-M_{13}M_{24}+M_{14}M_{23}\bigr)^{2}.$$
Substituting the values of Step 2,
$$M_{12}M_{34}-M_{13}M_{24}+M_{14}M_{23}=a_{34}a_{12}-(-a_{24})(-a_{13})+a_{23}a_{14}=a_{12}a_{34}-a_{13}a_{24}+a_{14}a_{23}=:\Pi.$$
Hence $\det A=\Pi^{2}$.

STEP 4. Computation of $\operatorname{vol}(\omega\wedge\omega)$.
Expanding $\omega\wedge\omega=\sum_{i<j}\sum_{k<l}a_{ij}a_{kl}\,e_i\wedge e_j\wedge e_k\wedge e_l$, a term is nonzero only if $\{i,j\}\cap\{k,l\}=\varnothing$. The surviving ordered pairs $((i,j),(k,l))$ are exactly $(12,34),(34,12),(13,24),(24,13),(14,23),(23,14)$, and by the sign rule of Step 2:
\begin{align*}
e_1\wedge e_2\wedge e_3\wedge e_4&=+E, & e_3\wedge e_4\wedge e_1\wedge e_2&=+E,\\
e_1\wedge e_3\wedge e_2\wedge e_4&=-E, & e_2\wedge e_4\wedge e_1\wedge e_3&=-E,\\
e_1\wedge e_4\wedge e_2\wedge e_3&=+E, & e_2\wedge e_3\wedge e_1\wedge e_4&=+E.\end{align*}
Consequently
$$\omega\wedge\omega=\bigl(2a_{12}a_{34}-2a_{13}a_{24}+2a_{14}a_{23}\bigr)E=2\Pi\,E,$$
and applying $\operatorname{vol}$ (with $\operatorname{vol}(E)=1$) gives
$$\operatorname{vol}(\omega\wedge\omega)=2\Pi.$$

STEP 5. Nondegeneracy versus invertibility of the matrix.
For $v=\sum_j x_j e_j$, the functional $B(\cdot,v)$ has coordinate row vector $Ax$ (i.e. $B(e_i,v)=\sum_j A_{ij}x_j$). Hence the right radical $\{v:B(\cdot,v)=0\}$ identifies with $\ker A$, and the left radical $\{v:B(v,\cdot)=0\}$ identifies with $\ker A^{\mathsf T}$. Since $A$ is a square matrix, $\ker A\ne 0\iff\det A=0$, and likewise for $A^{\mathsf T}$ (as $\det A^{\mathsf T}=\det A$). Thus $B$ is nondegenerate (both radicals trivial) if and only if $\det A\ne0$. Combined with Step 3, $B$ is nondegenerate $\iff\Pi\ne0$.

STEP 6. Conclusion.
The field $K$ has characteristic $0$, so $2\in K$ is nonzero and invertible; in particular $2\Pi\ne0\iff\Pi\ne0$.
($\Leftarrow$) Assume $B$ is nondegenerate. By Step 5, $\Pi\ne0$, and by Step 4, $\operatorname{vol}(\omega\wedge\omega)=2\Pi\ne0$.
($\Rightarrow$) Assume $\operatorname{vol}(\omega\wedge\omega)\ne0$. Then $2\Pi\ne0$, so $\Pi\ne0$ (as $2\ne0$ and $K$ is a field, hence a domain). By Step 5 (via Step 3, $\det A=\Pi^2\ne0$), $B$ is nondegenerate.

This establishes the equivalence in both directions, and all quantities appearing in the statement ($B$ and $\operatorname{vol}(\omega\wedge\omega)$) are defined independently of the basis chosen in Step 1, which was used only as a computational device. $\blacksquare$

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(d\ge2\), let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(Y\subsetneq X\) be a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) that is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\), and let \(j:U=X\setminus Y\hookrightarrow X\) be the open complement. Then \(H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell):=H^j(X_k,j_!\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for every integer \(j<d\).
proof:
We prove that H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=H^j(X_k,j_!\mathbb Q_\ell)=0 for every integer j<d.

STEP 0 (Setup and notation). Write i:Y\hookrightarrow X for the closed immersion and j:U=X\setminus Y\hookrightarrow X for the complementary open immersion; both are defined over \mathbb F_{q^m}. Put Q:=q^m=p^{am}, so that \mathbb F_{q^m}=\mathbb F_Q. The field k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q is algebraically closed of characteristic p, and \ell\neq p, so \ell\neq\operatorname{char}(k). Since X is projective (hence of finite type) over \mathbb F_{q^m}, the base changes X_k, Y_k and U_k are schemes of finite type over k. Since Y\subsetneq X is a nonempty effective Cartier divisor in the integral scheme X, it is a proper closed subscheme, and base change preserves complements: U_k=X_k\setminus Y_k.

We first record that the two possible readings of the group H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) coincide. Let j_k:U_k\hookrightarrow X_k be the base change of j. Extension by zero along an open immersion is computed on geometric stalks: for a geometric point \bar x\to X_k with image x\in X, the stalk of j_{k,!}\mathbb Q_\ell at \bar x is \mathbb Q_\ell if \bar x factors through U_k (equivalently x\in U) and 0 otherwise; this is exactly the stalk at \bar x of the pullback to X_k of j_!\mathbb Q_\ell on X. Hence j_{k,!}\mathbb Q_\ell\cong (j_!\mathbb Q_\ell)|_{X_k} as \mathbb Q_\ell-sheaves on X_{k,\mathrm{\acute et}}, and consequently
  H^j(X_{k,\mathrm{\acute et}},j_!\mathbb Q_\ell)\;=\;H^j(X_{k,\mathrm{\acute et}},j_{k,!}\mathbb Q_\ell)=:H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}((U_k),\mathbb Q_\ell).
So we may compute with the base-changed open immersion j_k.

STEP 1 (The Lefschetz hyperplane theorem for Y\subset X). The hypotheses of Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/258fa8 are satisfied verbatim: d\ge 2; X is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over \mathbb F_{q^m}; Y\subsetneq X is a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor defined over \mathbb F_{q^m}, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d-1; i:Y\hookrightarrow X is the closed immersion; \ell\neq p. That lemma yields, for every integer n with 0\le n\le d-1,
  (\dagger)_n\quad i^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\ \text{ is an isomorphism if } n<d-1,
  (\ddagger)\quad\quad i^*:H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\hookrightarrow H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\ \text{ is injective.}
(Recall that very ample implies ample, so this is the usual ample-divisor Lefschetz statement; we use the lemma exactly as stated, so no extra argument is needed.)

STEP 2 (The localisation long exact sequence over k). Apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_localization_les_finite_type to the algebraically closed field k, the prime \ell\neq\operatorname{char}(k)=p, the finite-type k-scheme X_k, the closed immersion i_k:Y_k\hookrightarrow X_k and the complementary open immersion j_k:U_k\hookrightarrow X_k. Its definition H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell):=H^m(X_{k,\mathrm{\acute et}},j_{k,!}\mathbb Q_\ell) agrees with the group of Step 0, and it gives a long exact sequence
  \cdots\to H^{n-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{i^*}H^{n-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{i^*}H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{n+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to\cdots
for every n\in\mathbb Z, in which the middle arrow is pullback along i_k.

STEP 3 (Short exact sequences cut out of the long one). Fix n\in\mathbb Z. Exactness at H^n_c(U_k):=:H^n_c and at H^n(X_k)=:H^n(X) gives
  \operatorname{im}\bigl[H^{n-1}(Y)\to H^n_c\bigr]=\ker\bigl[H^n_c\to H^n(X)\bigr],\qquad \operatorname{im}\bigl[H^n_c\to H^n(X)\bigr]=\ker\bigl[i^*:H^n(X)\to H^n(Y)\bigr],
and exactness at H^{n-1}(Y) gives \ker[H^{n-1}(Y)\to H^n_c]=\operatorname{im}[i^*:H^{n-1}(X)\to H^{n-1}(Y)]. By the first isomorphism theorem,
  \operatorname{im}\bigl[H^{n-1}(Y)\to H^n_c\bigr]\cong H^{n-1}(Y)\big/\operatorname{im}\bigl[i^*:H^{n-1}(X)\to H^{n-1}(Y)\bigr]=\operatorname{coker}\bigl(i^*_{n-1}\bigr).
Assembling these identifications yields a canonical short exact sequence of \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces
  (\ast)\qquad 0\longrightarrow \operatorname{coker}\bigl(i^*_{n-1}\bigr)\longrightarrow H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow \ker\bigl(i^*_n\bigr)\longrightarrow 0,
where i^*_m denotes i^*:H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

STEP 4 (Vanishing for 0\le n\le d-1). Let n be an integer with 0\le n\le d-1; we show both outer terms of (\ast) vanish.

(a) The cokernel term. If n=0 then H^{-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0=H^{-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), because these are the derived functors R^m\Gamma of the left-exact functor \Gamma applied to the sheaves \mathbb Q_\ell and j_{k,!}\mathbb Q_\ell, and R^m\Gamma=0 for m<0; hence \operatorname{coker}(i^*_{-1})=0. If n\ge 1, then 0\le n-1\le d-2<d-1 and also n-1\le d-1, so (\dagger)_{n-1} applies and i^*_{n-1} is an isomorphism; therefore \operatorname{coker}(i^*_{n-1})=0.

(b) The kernel term. If n\le d-2, then 0\le n<d-1 and n\le d-1, so (\dagger)_n applies: i^*_n is an isomorphism, in particular injective, hence \ker(i^*_n)=0. If n=d-1, then (\ddagger) says precisely that i^*_{d-1} is injective, hence \ker(i^*_{d-1})=0.

Both outer terms of (\ast) are zero, so the middle term is zero: H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0 for every 0\le n\le d-1.

STEP 5 (Negative degrees). If j<0, then H^j(X_k,j_!\mathbb Q_\ell)=0, since j_!\mathbb Q_\ell is a single sheaf (a complex concentrated in degree 0) and étale cohomology, being R^j\Gamma of a sheaf, vanishes for j<0.

STEP 6 (Conclusion). Let j<d be an arbitrary integer. If j<0, Step 5 gives H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0. If 0\le j, then j\le d-1 because d is an integer and j<d, so Step 4 gives H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0. In both cases the group vanishes, which is exactly the required conclusion.

REMARK ON THE HYPOTHESES. The assumption d\ge 2 is used to invoke the Lefschetz lemma of Step 1 (which requires d\ge 2); the assumption that Y is a very ample Cartier divisor, nonempty, defined over \mathbb F_{q^m}, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d-1 is used exactly as the hypothesis of that lemma; smoothness and projectivity of X are used only through that lemma and to ensure X_k is of finite type over k, which is all the localisation lemma needs. No use is made of the Frobenius structure.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, \(\ell\neq p\) prime, \(m\ge1\), \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(Y\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(\mathcal E\) be a vector bundle of rank \(\rho\ge1\) on \(Y\) defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and let \(\pi:P=\mathbf P_Y(\mathcal E)\to Y\) be the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients. If the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}\), is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\), then it is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\), and its scalar extension to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is diagonalizable.
proof:
Notation and setup. Put Q := q^m = p^{am}; this is again a prime power, and k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q = \overline{\mathbb F}_{q^m}. Write \sigma:k\to k, \sigma(c)=c^{Q}=c^{q^m}. For a scheme Z over \mathbb F_{q^m} we write F_Z := (\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^* for the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius acting on H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell); by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a (applied to the prime power Q and the \mathbb F_{q^m}-schemes Y and P) each F_Z is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphism of H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every i\ge 0. We write H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell):=0 for j<0 (negative étale cohomology groups of a sheaf vanish), so that all direct sums below are finite and unambiguously defined. The rank of \mathcal E is \rho\ge 1; set r := \rho-1\ge 0, so \rho = r+1. The projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients is P=\mathbf P_Y(\mathcal E)=\operatorname{Proj}(\operatorname{Sym}_{\mathcal O_Y}\mathcal E), with structural morphism \pi:P\to Y and tautological line bundle \mathcal O(1).

Step 1 (finite-dimensionality of the cohomology of Y and of P). The variety Y is projective over \mathbb F_{q^m}, hence proper over \mathbb F_{q^m}; P = \operatorname{Proj}(\operatorname{Sym}\mathcal E) is projective over Y, and the composition P\to Y\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^m} is therefore proper. Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob over the prime power Q, with X equal to Y (respectively P) and with K the constant sheaf \mathbb Q_\ell on X_k equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism \psi:F_X^*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell (which is precisely the datum the lemma requires). The lemma gives, for every integer n, that H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell, and that the induced canonical Frobenius automorphism coincides with F_X. Hence:
  (1a) each H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell, and F_Y is an invertible \mathbb Q_\ell-linear operator on it;
  (1b) each H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell, and F_P is an invertible \mathbb Q_\ell-linear operator on it.

Step 2 (Frobenius-equivariant projective bundle formula, degree by degree). Fix an integer n\ge 0 once and for all; this n stays fixed through Steps 3-6.
