Fix a nonzero \tau\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1) and let c\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) be the class of \mathcal O(1) as in Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_307. Applying that lemma with the prime power Q in place of its q (its hypotheses are satisfied: Y is smooth, projective and geometrically connected over \mathbb F_{q^m}, \mathcal E is a vector bundle of rank r+1\ge 1 defined over \mathbb F_{q^m}, and P is the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients), we obtain a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism
\[
\Phi_n:\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r} H^{\,n-2i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad (x_0,\dots,x_r)\longmapsto \sum_{i=0}^{r}\pi^*x_i\cup c^{\,i}.
\]
Moreover Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_307 asserts that this isomorphism carries the direct-sum operator \bigoplus_{i=0}^{r} Q^{\,i}F_Y on the left to F_P on the right; written out, with T_n:=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r} Q^{\,i}F_Y acting on V_n:=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r} H^{\,n-2i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),
\[
\Phi_n\circ T_n \;=\; F_P\circ\Phi_n .
\tag{2.1}
\n(Concretely: \pi is defined over \mathbb F_{q^m}, so F_P\circ\pi^*=\pi^*\circ F_Y; c is the cycle class of the \mathbb F_{q^m}-rational line bundle \mathcal O(1), so F_P(c)=Q\,c (the Tate-twist factor, the pullback of \tau under c\mapsto c^{Q}); and cup product is functorial for pullback, whence F_P(\pi^*x_i\cup c^i)=\pi^*(F_Yx_i)\cup Q^i c^i, which is exactly (2.1).)

Step 3 (finite-dimensionality of V_n, for this same fixed n). The index set \{0,\dots,r\} has r+1=\rho terms, and for each i the space H^{\,n-2i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell by (1a) (it is 0 when n-2i<0, which is also finite-dimensional). Hence V_n is a finite direct sum of finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces, so V_n is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell. Together with (1b) this supplies exactly the finite-dimensionality hypotheses needed for the linear-algebra lemmas used in Steps 4-6.

Step 4 (each summand operator Q^i F_Y is semisimple). Fix i with 0\le i\le r and put W_i:=H^{\,n-2i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and T:=F_Y|_{W_i}, an invertible operator by (1a). If W_i=0 there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, Q^i\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times} (Q=p^{am}\ge 2 is invertible in \mathbb Q_\ell), and we claim that T semisimple implies Q^i T semisimple. Indeed, apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5 to the finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-space W_i: T is semisimple on W_i if and only if T_{\bar{\mathbb Q}_\ell} is diagonalizable on W_i\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell. If T_{\bar{\mathbb Q}_\ell} is diagonalizable, then W_i\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell=\bigoplus_{\lambda}E_\lambda is the eigenspace decomposition, and (Q^i T)_{\bar{\mathbb Q}_\ell} acts on each E_\lambda as the scalar Q^i\lambda; hence it is again diagonalizable, and applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5 in the reverse direction gives that Q^i T is semisimple on W_i. (The converse uses the same argument with Q^{-i}.) By the hypothesis of the present lemma, F_Y is semisimple on H^{\,n-2i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every degree, in particular on W_i; hence Q^{\,i}F_Y is semisimple on W_i for every i=0,\dots,r. Each Q^{\,i}F_Y is invertible by (1a) and Q^i\ne 0.

Step 5 (the direct sum is semisimple). By Step 4, each of the \rho invertible operators Q^{\,i}F_Y\in\mathrm{GL}(W_i) is semisimple. Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_9 to the finite-dimensional spaces W_0,\dots,W_r (finite-dimensional by Step 3) and these operators, the direct-sum operator T_n=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}Q^{\,i}F_Y is semisimple on V_n.

Step 6 (transport to P via the intertwining isomorphism). Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8 with V=V_n, W=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), T_V=T_n, T_W=F_P and \alpha=\Phi_n. All hypotheses hold: V and W are finite-dimensional (Step 3 and (1b)), T_V and T_W are invertible (Steps 4-5 and (1a)-(1b), eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a), \alpha is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism (Step 2), and \alpha\circ T_V=T_W\circ\alpha is exactly (2.1). Since T_V is semisimple by Step 5, eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8 yields that F_P is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

Step 7 (diagonalizability after scalar extension). Now apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5 to the finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space V=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) (finite-dimensional by (1b)) and the operator T=F_P. The semisimplicity just proved in Step 6 is equivalent, by that lemma, to the statement that the scalar extension F_P\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell} of F_P to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell is diagonalizable. This is the second conclusion required.

Step 8 (all degrees, edge cases). The integer n\ge 0 was fixed arbitrarily at the start of Step 2 and never specialised; Steps 3-7 were carried out for that arbitrary n using only the isomorphism \Phi_n, which Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_307 provides for every n\ge 0 with no vanishing hypothesis. Hence F_P=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*, \sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every n\ge 0, and its scalar extension to \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell is diagonalizable for every n\ge 0. No vanishing theorem is invoked. The two conventions already recorded are what cover the boundary cases: for degrees with n-2i<0 the corresponding summand is the zero space (Step 2's convention), and in the rank-one case \rho=1 (i.e. r=0) the direct sum has the single summand i=0 and \Phi_0=\pi^* is the usual isomorphism H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), while the single operator F_Y is semisimple by hypothesis. This completes the proof. \hfill\qedsymbol
